spans.Background: The Product Line Architecture (PLA) design is a multi-objective optimization problem that can be properly solved with search-based algorithms. However, search-based PLA design is an incipient research ﬁeld. Due to this, works in this ﬁeld have addressed main points to solve the problem: adequate representation, speciﬁc search operators and suitable evaluation ﬁtness functions. Similarly what happens in the search-based design of traditional software, existing works on search-based PLA design use NSGA-II, without evaluating the characteristics of this algorithm, such as the use of crossover operator.
spans.Objective: this paper reports results from a comparative analysis of two algorithms, NSGA-II and PAES, to the PLA design problem.
spans.Methods: An experimental study was carried out with nine PLAs
spans.Results: results of the conducted study attest that NSGA-II performs better than PAES in the PLA design context.
spans.ProblemStatement: Empirical results, reported in the search- based software design [21], [22], observed that the crossover operator does not offer signiﬁcant advantage, when it is implemented in a random fashion. Similarly, to solve the PLA design problem with MOEAs, it is possible to use either algorithms by deﬁning a speciﬁc crossover operator, or an algorithm that does not employ crossover. These options have not been evaluated in the SPL context.
spans.ResearchObjectives: the main contribution of this paper is reporting results from a comparative analysis of two MOEAs in the PLA design optimization, providing some insights about the importance of the crossover operation in such context.
spans.Context: The Software Product Line (SPL) approach comprises techniques for systematically creating similar software sys- tems from a shared set of software assets. A ﬂexible and reusable Product Line Architecture (PLA) enables large- scale reuse [1]. Hence, PLA is a fundamental SPL asset, since it entails a design that is common to every product derived from the SPL. Such design includes components to realize common and variable features. A feature [2] is a system property or functionality that is relevant to some SPL stakeholder and is used to capture commonalities among systems or discriminate them.
spans.Goals: Analyze the solutions sets obtained by the MOEAs, PAES and NSGA-II (using or not the crossover operator) for the purpose of evaluating with respect to their diversity and the best trade-off between the objectives from the point of view of the researcher in the context of search-based PLA design.
spans.ExperimentalUnits: The experimental study involved nine PLA designs ... AGM-1 ... AGM-2 ... AGM-3 ... AGM-4 ... MM-1 ... MM-2 ... MM-3 ... MM-4 ... LPS-BET
spans.ExperimentalMaterial: To perform the study, we extended the framework jMetal [40] to deal with PLA design. ... conﬁgurations with populations formed by 100 individuals ... the mutation rate was tuned using three conﬁgurations: {0.8, 0.9, 1.0}
spans.Tasks: Empirical tuning procedures were conducted with AGM-1 and AGM-3 for NSGA-II and PAES according to [42] aiming at deﬁning the population size, mutation rate and crossover rate. The tuning results were compared using the indicator HV. Firstly, the population size was tested and conﬁgurations with populations formed by 100 individuals covered conﬁgurations using 50 and 70 individuals for both algorithms. So, the population size for the NSGA- II versions and the external archive size for PAES were set as 100. Secondly, the mutation rate was tuned using three conﬁgurations: {0.8, 0.9, 1.0}. Solutions achieved with the rate 0.9 outperformed solutions found by the other conﬁgurations for both MOEAs. Finally, the crossover rate was empirically adjusted for NSGA-II. The value 0.1 outper- formed the other tested values: {0.2, 0.04}. The values tested in the parameters tuning were extracted from experiments conducted in [12], [14], [18], [19]. The maximum number of generations was set as 300 and it was used as stop criterion for all algorithms. Each experiment was executed 30 times for each PLA in order to know the behavior of each algorithm to solve the problem [43].
spans.Hypotheses: The main hypothesis of the study is the null hypothesis (H0) that states there is no difference between both MOEAs. Therefore, the study tries to reject this hypothesis. Addition- ally, alternative hypotheses (H1 and H2) are deﬁned to be accepted when the null hypothesis is rejected. H1 states that NSGA-II has better performance than PAES with respect to HV and ED and vice-versa for H2. These hypotheses are deﬁned below in terms of indicators measured to conduct the comparison: HV and ED. H0: HV NSGA−II = HV P AES and EDNSGA−II = EDP AES H1: HV NSGA−II > HV P AES and EDNSGA−II < EDP AES H2: HV NSGA−II < HV P AES and EDNSGA−II > EDP AES
spans.IndependentVariables: The independent variables are the two MOEAs NSGA-II and PAES. Additionally, for NSGA-II, the set of genetic operators applied is another independent variable in order to analyse the performance of NSGA-II with and without crossover against PAES. The ﬁrst set includes only the mutation operators for PLA design described in Section II, and does not include any crossover operator. This version is named NSGAII-M. The second set includes the mutation operators and the feature-driven crossover (Section II). This version is called NSGAII-MC.
spans.DependentVariables: The dependent variables in the experiment are the ﬁtness of the solutions, the diversity of the solutions and the best trade-off between the objectives.
spans.Procedure: To perform the study, we extended the framework jMetal [40] to deal with PLA design. Figure 2 depicts the main classes created (highlighted in gray) to do this. The problem OPLA specializes the jMetal problem. OPLA uses conventionalMetrics and feature-drivenMetrics in the optimization of variables of the type Architecture. The class ArchitectureSolutionType was added to allow the manipulation of PLAs. The input is an XMI ﬁle contain- ing a PLA design modeled in a UML class diagram. The PLA representation is instantiated to an object of the class Architecture from this XMI ﬁle. The obtained solutions containing the PLA designs are also saved as XMI ﬁles. ... Empirical tuning procedures were conducted with AGM-1 and AGM-3 for NSGA-II and PAES according to [42] aiming at deﬁning the population size, mutation rate and crossover rate. The tuning results were compared using the indicator HV. Firstly, the population size was tested and conﬁgurations with populations formed by 100 individuals covered conﬁgurations using 50 and 70 individuals for both algorithms. So, the population size for the NSGA- II versions and the external archive size for PAES were set as 100. Secondly, the mutation rate was tuned using three conﬁgurations: {0.8, 0.9, 1.0}. Solutions achieved with the rate 0.9 outperformed solutions found by the other conﬁgurations for both MOEAs. Finally, the crossover rate was empirically adjusted for NSGA-II. The value 0.1 outper- formed the other tested values: {0.2, 0.04}. The values tested in the parameters tuning were extracted from experiments conducted in [12], [14], [18], [19]. The maximum number of generations was set as 300 and it was used as stop criterion for all algorithms. ... Each experiment was executed 30 times for each PLA in order to know the behavior of each algorithm to solve the problem [43].
spans.AnalysisProcedure: In our study, we use the indicators HV and ED (Section III) for quantifying the diversity of the solutions and measuring the best trade-off between the objectives, respectively. Friedman statistical test [33] was used at a 5% signiﬁcance level (p-value <= 0.05) in order to verify the statistical difference between the MOEAs. It is a non-parametric statistical test used to compare multiple data sets. After, the post hoc test [34] from R tool [35] was applied, using the package pgirmess. The post hoc test identiﬁes which MOEA obtained the best average values.
spans.Summary: In this work we report results on a comparative analysis of two MOEAs, NSGA-II and PAES, in the search-based PLA design. To do this, we used a multi-objective approach that employs two objectives based on conventional and feature- driven metrics to evaluate the quality of the achieved solu- tions. Such approach includes a speciﬁc crossover operator, and conventional and feature-driven mutation operators. Empirical results show that, in our study, NSGA-II outper- forms PAES for solving the referred problem with respect to the diversity of the solutions and the best trade-off between the objectives. In addition to this, the use of crossover seems to be a good option in the investigated context.
spans.FutureWork: As future work, we intend to ask the opinion of the orig- inal PLA designers about the quality of obtained solutions. The use of other ﬁtness functions and different number of objectives in the PLA design context should be investigated, as well as other algorithms.

spans.Background: Analyzing software product lines is difﬁcult, due to their inherent variability. In the past, several strategies for product-line analysis have been proposed, in particular, product-based, feature-based, and family-based strategies. Despite recent attempts to conceptu- ally and empirically compare different strategies, there is no work that empirically compares all of the three strategies in a controlled setting.
spans.Objective: We close this gap by extending a compiler for feature- oriented programming with support for product-based, feature- based, and family-based type checking.
spans.Methods: We present and discuss the results of a comparative performance evaluation that we con- ducted on a set of 12 feature-oriented, JAVA-based product lines.
spans.Results: Most notably, we found that the family-based strategy is superior for all subject product lines: it is substantially faster, it detects all kinds of errors, and provides the most detailed information about them.
spans.ProblemStatement: Despite existing empirical work on product-line analysis, there is no any study that compared all three strategies in a controlled setting (i.e., by means of a common set of subject systems and the same analysis tool that implements all three strategies).
spans.ResearchObjectives: Our goal is to close this gap. As a concrete analysis technique, we chose type checking, as it has been used before in several studies on product- line analysis [3, 14, 18, 21]. As an implementation technique, we use feature-oriented programming [6], because we already have a proper tool infrastructure at our disposal, and we have access to a repository of subject systems for our experiments.
spans.Context: A feature is an end-user-visible behavior or characteristic of a prod- uct that satisﬁes a stakeholder’s requirement [17]. A software prod- uct line is a family of related software products that share common features and differ in other features [12]. The product-line approach introduces a further dimension of complexity to software engineer- ing: variability. It is this additional dimension that renders existing analysis tools impractical, for example, model checkers, static an- alyzers, type checkers, and so on [30]. Sure, to analyze a product line, we can use an off-the-shelf analysis tool and apply it to all of its products, which, however, requires exponential analysis ef- fort, due to feature combinatorics (in the worst case, the number of products grows exponentially with the number of features). Alter- natively, applying off-the-shelf tools to the variable code base of a product line itself (e.g., consisting of unprocessed C code, feature modules, or aspects) is often impossible. However, a solution is to make the tools variability-aware [30].
spans.Goals: The main goal of our evaluation is to compare the three strategies quantitatively in terms of their performance.
spans.ExperimentalUnits: We conducted the evaluation of the type-checking strategies on a set of 12 feature-oriented, JAVA-based product lines. The set has been collected and prepared before for benchmarking purposes and was used in several studies [1, 5]. The subject systems belong to different application domains, and they are of different sizes: in terms of lines of code, number of features, and number of prod- ucts. In Section 3.6, we use the three size categories to discuss the relation between the size of a product line and the corresponding performance of type checking. Table 2 summarizes relevant infor- mation about the systems.
spans.ExperimentalMaterial: We conducted all measurements on a workstation equipped with an Intel Xeon CPU (2.9 GHz) and 8 GB RAM, running Ubuntu 12.04 (64-Bit) and OpenJDK 7 (u21).
spans.Hypotheses: Based on our previous considerations, we state the following three hypotheses that we address in the evaluation: H.1: The family-based strategy is superior to the feature-based and product-based strategies in terms of performance. H.2: As an exception to H.1, the product-based strategy is superior to the family-based one, if the analyzed product line has a relatively small number of products. H.3: As an exception to H.1, the feature-based strategy is supe- rior to the family-based one, if the analyzed product line has a relatively small number of features.
spans.IndependentVariables: the three type-checking strategies—family-based, feature-based, and product-based—
spans.DependentVariables: performance ... the time required by every step of the type-checking procedure (i.e., tsetup and tchecking)
spans.Procedure: To compare the performance of the three type-checking strategies, we applied each strategy to each subject system, and we measured the time required by every step of the type-checking procedure (i.e., tsetup and tchecking). We repeated each measurement 10 times and took the average value to reduce measurement bias. The maximum relative standard error was 3.1 %, which we observed for family- based type checking of ZIPME. For the product-based strategy, we did not include the time needed to generate the conﬁguration of each product, because this time was negligible compared to the time required for type checking. Likewise, for the feature-based strategy, we did not include the time used to generate stubs (Sec- tion 2.4), because stubs represent required interfaces and are part of the corresponding feature modules. We measured the performance of the family-based type checker twice, with and without caching, to investigate the inﬂuence of the caching (Section 3.2) on the over- all performance. We instrumented the code of the FUJI compiler with calls to the timer of ThreadMXBean,4 such that we measure only the CPU time consumed by the type-checker thread. This approach eliminates the inﬂuence of other concurrent tasks (e.g., garbage collection) on the measurement results. Furthermore, we did not measure the JVM startup time for each type-checking run, because the overhead can be avoided using special tools.
spans.Summary: For the ﬁrst time, we compared the three product-line analysis strategies—product-based, feature-based, and family-based—in a controlled setting. In our evaluation, we used feature-oriented pro- gramming as an implementation technique and type checking as an analysis technique, although the big picture of our results may be transferable to other techniques. In particular, we compared the analysis performance, but we also addressed the ability to detect different kinds of errors, and the quality of the provided information about errors. Our evaluation is based on a feature-oriented com- piler that we extended with the three type-checking strategies for this purpose, and a subject set of 12 feature-oriented, JAVA-based product lines. A main result of our study is that the family-based strategy outperforms the other strategies for all subject systems in terms of analysis time. We identiﬁed its caching mechanism as the key factor for the success, as it substantially reduces the number of SAT-solver queries. At the same time, the family-based strategy is complete: it ﬁnds errors that are feature-local and that occur between features (556 in total), which is not the case for the feature- based strategy. Furthermore, the family-based strategy provides the most comprehensive error messages, as it has all information on features and variability at its disposal, which is not the case for the other two strategies. Although not being in the focus of our study, we found that pursuing a sampling-based strategy (checking only a tractable sub- set of products) would not change the big picture. For our subject systems, the break-even point, at which the family-based strategy becomes faster, is at very low numbers of products, which means that the corresponding analysis coverage of sampling is likely to be very small, compared to the family-based strategy, which achieves full coverage. Surprisingly, the feature-based strategy is often slower than the family-based strategy, although it ignores feature interactions and is, consequently, incomplete. Combining the feature-based with the product-based strategy makes it complete, but is substantially slower. Interestingly, such a combined strategy outperforms the plain product-based strategy in most cases in our experiments, which indicates that separate feature compilation and byte-code composition can have a positive effect on analysis performance.
spans.FutureWork: An interesting avenue of further work is to combine the individ- ual strategies and to explore trade-offs in the search for an optimal strategy [32].

Surprisingly, the feature-based strategy is often slower than the family-based strategy, although it ignores feature interactions and is, consequently, incomplete. Combining the feature-based with the product-based strategy makes it complete, but is substantially slower. Interestingly, such a combined strategy outperforms the plain product-based strategy in most cases in our experiments, which indicates that separate feature compilation and byte-code composition can have a positive effect on analysis performance.",

}

spans.Background: Feature models are often used to describe variability and commonality in Software Product Lines, specifying admissible configurations of valid products. However, invalid configurations may arise in some scenarios. These include feature model evolution that invalidates pre-existing products or collaborative configuration by multiple stakeholders with conflicting goals, among others. This problem has been acknowledged in the literature and some techniques for configuration repair have already been proposed.
spans.Objective: We offer a novel approach for configuration repair, based on partitioning and cover analysis, with high performance and generating high quality solutions, which allows efficient identification and presentation of multiple competing repairs.
spans.ProblemStatement: Any valid configuration must conform to the structure of the feature tree and constraints included in the feature model. Invalid configurations may, however, arise in many different scenarios, such as: ... Feature model evolution. ... Shared configuration by multiple stakeholders. ... Configuration by untrained stakeholders. ... In these situations, automated support for transforming an invalid configuration into a valid one (i.e., repairing the configuration) can be invaluable.
spans.ResearchObjectives: We propose a novel approach to configuration repair, based on partitioning of the feature model and cover extraction, for addressing the problem of configuration repair.
spans.Context: Software Product Line (SPL) development is an approach based on the planned reuse of code, models, requirements and other artefacts for creating products within a well-defined domain. A product is created by defining a valid configuration of features, which will in turn determine what assets should be composed for creating the product. Feature models are often used to represent the commonality and variability of products. These specify valid configurations, by means of constraints and a feature tree including mandatory, optional and grouped features.
spans.Goals: The objective of the experiments is to assess the performance, scalability and effectiveness of our approach in identifying repairs and being able to offer a manageable and understandable perspective of the repairs to the user.
spans.ExperimentalUnits: a set of the largest non-synthetic models available in the SPLOT online feature model repository.
spans.ExperimentalMaterial: All tests were run on a Windows 7 64 bit machine, with a 2 GHz Core-i7 processor and 8 Gb RAM. The Espresso-MV tool was used to perform minimization of the cover.
spans.Tasks: Partitioning and cover computation. This is a critical operation that must be performed only once for each feature model, before the initial repair is obtained. Subsequent repairs for any initial configurations can be obtained reusing the cover data, so recomputation is not required. ... Repairing random invalid configurations. In this set of experiments, invalid initial configurations are generated and then repaired. Invalid configurations are created by a simple process based on iterative generation and inspection of random configurations, until an invalid configuration is found. Multiple are may be conducted over the same feature model, using different initial defective configurations. We also take this opportunity to explore the repair of partially specified configurations and alternative assessment criteria. ... Offering a manageable perspective of repairs. In this set of experiments, we examine the suitability of our approach for successfully decomposing the required repairs into a set of disjoint problems. The rate of success is measured by comparing the total number of possible repairs (as would be shown in an exhaustive list) with the number of subproblems identified.
spans.DependentVariables: performance, scalability and effectiveness
spans.Procedure: All tests were run on a Windows 7 64 bit machine, with a 2 GHz Core-i7 processor and 8 Gb RAM. The Espresso-MV tool was used to perform minimization of the cover.
spans.Summary: We presented our approach for the repair of invalid configurations, based on partition and analysis of the cover of the feature model. We have conducted a series of experiments to validate our approach that confirmed good performance. We also described an approach to decompose the possible repairs into a modest number of sub-problems that can be independently analyzed and resolved by the user, allowing manageable analysis and resolution of scenarios where thousands or even millions of alternative optimal repairs are possible. Our approach demonstrated not only excellent performance, but also allows different repair selection criteria to be used and the ability to seamlessly handle partially specified configurations. Multiple optimal solutions are efficiently identified and retrieved.
spans.FutureWork: Several areas of future research have been identified: ... Extending the work into other variability models such as CDL or Kconfig. ... The Espresso-MV algorithm is the state-of-the-art logic minimizer. Even though some graphical user interfaces have been since developed, the public sources haven’t been maintained since the late 80s (a small cleanup was made in the early 90s). A revision could address stability issues found when handling one specific example. ... Optimal repairs were demonstrated to be generated even if non-optimal covers are used (Section 4.2). Aggressive partitioning approaches, trading off cover optimality for scalability, can be explored.

spans.Background: However, previous empirical studies optimized PLA design using the multi-objective and evolutionary algorithm NSGA-II, without applying one of the most important genetic operators: the crossover.
spans.Objective: this paper presents a feature-driven crossover operator that aims at improving feature mod- ularization in PLA design.
spans.Methods: The proposed operator was applied in two empirical studies using NSGA-II in comparison with another version of NSGA-II that uses only mutation operators.
spans.Results: The results show the usefulness and applicability of the proposed operator.
spans.Conclusions: The NSGA-II version that applies the feature-driven crossover found a greater diversity of solutions (potential PLA designs), with higher feature-based cohesion, and less feature scattering and tangling.
spans.ProblemStatement: Existing crossover operators proposed in those works could be adapted to the context of PLA design. But, they are not concerned with feature modularization, what is important for PLA design.
spans.ResearchObjectives: in this paper, we describe a feature-driven crossover operator and study its beneﬁts to PLA design optimization. The main goal is to employ crossover and mutation operators of MOGAs together when using the MOA4PLA approach.
spans.Context: We can hypothesize that a speciﬁc crossover operator that considers fea- ture modularization is a more valuable contribution for search based PLA design than to adapt existing crossover operators to the current context.
spans.Goals: In the ﬁrst study we was interested in validating the usefulness of the pro- posed operator ... The goal of this new study is to evaluate the impact of the crossover operator in diﬀerent combinations of objectives.
spans.ExperimentalUnits: They were conducted with a supporting tool, named OPLA-Tool [38] and nine PLAs. ... Arcade Game Maker (AGM) [40] is a SPL ... Mobile Media (MM) [37] is a SPL ... LPS-BET [41] supports the bus city transport management. ... MOA4PLA ... two versions of the MOGA NSGA-II [18]
spans.ExperimentalMaterial: They were conducted with a supporting tool, named OPLA-Tool [38] and nine PLAs. ... We decided to start the PLA design optimization considering only the static structural aspect of the architecture, expressible as a UML (stereo- typed) class diagram. ... To analyze the results three diﬀerent sets of solutions are generally used [43].
spans.Tasks: The ﬁrst version implements an asexual method (only mutation operators) and the second version uses both mutation and feature-driven crossover.
spans.Hypotheses: In the ﬁrst study, two traditional ﬁtness functions, based on feature mod- ularization and design principles, were used and we hypothesized that the feature-driven crossover provides beneﬁts to PLA design.
spans.Parameters: We performed an empirical parameters tuning to set our experiments. This tuning was performed to AGM-1 and MM-1. The obtained results were compared in terms of coverage as described below. Three diﬀerent population sizes were tested: {50, 70, 100}. Experiments using populations formed by 100 individuals achieved better performance. Those values for population size are the same experimented in related work [29, 15] and it is interesting to highlight that this parameter was set equal those works. Larger populations have lower diversity due to the size of PLA designs used in the experiments. The generations number was set as 300 due to the population convergence measured by both no change in best ﬁtness and lack of variation in genotypes. The mutation rate was tuned using three conﬁgurations: {0.8, 0.9, 1.0}. Solutions achieved with the rate 0.9 outperformed solutions found by the other conﬁgurations. The crossover rate was also empirically adjusted for NSGAII-MC. The value 0.1 outperformed the other tested values: {0.2, 0.04}. It is important to highlight that in search based PLA design, as well as in search based design, mutation rates are high and crossover rates are low [13, 15]. ... The same parameters tuning of the Study 1 was adopted in Study 2. The only exception was the probability of the feature-driven mutation operator application. The six mutation operators had the same application probability in the ﬁrst study. However, it was noticed as a result of Study 1 that if the feature-driven mutation operator were applied a greater number of times, better feature modularization would be achieved. So, in the second study, the probability of application of feature-driven mutation was doubled aiming at obtaining PLA designs with a greater feature modularization.
spans.Procedure: The studies were conducted with a supporting tool, named OPLA-Tool [38] and nine PLAs. Each experiment was executed 30 independent runs for each PLA as recommended in [42], in order to reduce the possibility of the results were obtained by chance since search algorithms includes random variations. The number of ﬁtness evaluations was used as stop criterion.
spans.Summary: In this paper we presented a feature-driven crossover operator to optimize PLA design with multi-objective and evolutionary algorithms. In previous works only mutation operators were used, and the proposed crossover allows to explore all the potential of those algorithms. In addition to this, the crossover is driven to feature modularization. It generates a new PLA design from two parents by swapping groups of architectural elements which realize a particular feature. To evaluate the usefulness and applicability of the proposed operator we conducted two studies, with the approach MOA4PLA and two versions of NSGA-II: one using only mutation operators, and other using mutation operators and the feature-driven crossover operator. In the ﬁrst study, two traditional ﬁtness functions, based on feature modularization and design principles, were used and we hypothesized that the feature-driven crossover provides beneﬁts to PLA design. The results of the conducted study corroborate to our hypothesis. Feature-driven crossover allows NSGA-II ﬁnd better solutions in terms of ﬁtness and higher diversity of solutions. A qualitative analysis showed the operator also provides solutions with higher quality in terms of feature-based cohesion and feature scattering and tangling. In the second study, two diﬀerent combinations of ﬁtness functions were used. Again, we obtained beneﬁcial impact of the crossover when using a pair formed of feature modularization and, cohesion and coupling metrics. As mentioned before, PLA extensibility did not change for the conﬁguration of the second study using those PLA designs. However, in PLAs with diﬀerent characteristics, the extensibility could be improved. In this sense, other studies would be performed involving diﬀerent PLA designs. Some lessons were learned during the studies conduction. One of them points out a limitation of the proposed operator to maintain the consistency of some obtained solutions.
spans.FutureWork: As future work, we intend to improve the feature-driven crossover to settle its lim- itations. For doing that, we will perform a qualitative analysis of the results to investigate other points that need to be treated by the feature-driven crossover. We also intend to ask the opinion of the original PLA designers about the quality of obtained solutions. Thus, it will be possible to improve the feature-driven crossover encompassing drawbacks pointed by the designers.

spans.Background: The Product Line Architecture (PLA) design is a multi-objective optimization problem that can be properly solved in the Search Based Software Engineering (SBSE) ﬁeld. However, the PLA design has speciﬁc characteristics. For example, the PLA is designed in terms of features and a highly modular PLA is necessary to enable the growth of a software product line.
spans.Objective: this paper introduces a feature-driven crossover operator that aims at improving feature modularization.
spans.Methods: The proposed operator was applied in an empirical study using the multi-objective evolutionary algorithm named NSGAII.
spans.Limitations: The Product Line Architecture (PLA) design is a multi-objective optimization problem that can be properly solved in the Search Based Software Engineering (SBSE) ﬁeld. However, the PLA design has speciﬁc characteristics. For example, the PLA is designed in terms of features and a highly modular PLA is necessary to enable the growth of a software product line. However, existing search based design approaches do not consider such needs.
spans.Conclusions: In comparison with another version of NSGAII that uses only mutation operators, the feature-driven crossover version found a greater diversity of solutions (potential PLA designs), with higher feature-based cohesion, and less feature scattering and tangling.
spans.ProblemStatement: However, features are rarely modularized. Modularizing features is difﬁcult because feature-speciﬁc code often cuts across class boundaries. Even so, it is natural to consider modularizing features as a way to modularize programs [21]. Thus, the higher feature modularization the lower functionality scatter- ing in PLA design. Feature modularization also affects other modularity topics, such as cohesion, coupling, crosscutting and tangling [11]. Metrics for PLA design evaluation provide indicators about modularity topics [2], [16], [26]. Neverthe- less, architects need to analyse a lot of metric values. So, ﬁnding the best trade-off among the used metrics to deﬁne PLA design becomes a people-intensive task. Furthermore, some metrics can be in conﬂict and architects need to choose which metric should be prioritized.
spans.ResearchObjectives: in this paper, we propose a feature-driven crossover operator and study its beneﬁts to PLA design optimization. The research question that guides our study is whether the feature-driven crossover provides beneﬁts when optimizing PLA design using MOEAs.
spans.Context: Software Product Line (SPL) approach focuses on the development of speciﬁc products within a well-deﬁned domain by leveraging their commonalities and managing their variabilities in a systematic way. Organizations have adopted SPL approach in order to shift from the reuse of individual components to the large-scale reuse of a product- line architecture (PLA) [20]. PLA is the SPL main core asset since it entails a design that is common to all the products derived from the SPL. Such design includes components to realize common and variable features.
spans.Goals: We performed an empirical study applying NSGAII-M and NSGAII-MC for nine PLA designs aiming at comparing the obtained results.
spans.ExperimentalUnits: Arcade Game Maker (AGM) [28] ... Mobile Media (MM) [10] ... LPS-BET [13] ... We executed two experiments to evaluate the proposed crossover: NSGAII-M and NSGAII-MC.
spans.ExperimentalMaterial: The input is an XMI ﬁle containing a PLA design modeled in a UML class diagram. ... To analyze the results of the empirical study three different sets of solutions were used. The ﬁrst one is PFapprox. ... The second set is PFknown. ... The last one is PFtrue.
spans.Tasks: To perform the study, we extended the jMetal frame- work [14] and implemented the most used MOEA NSGAII (Non-dominated Sorting Genetic Algorithm) [12]. ... The input is an XMI ﬁle containing a PLA design modeled in a UML class diagram. The PLA representation is instantiated from the XMI ﬁle given as input. ... We executed two experiments to evaluate the proposed crossover: NSGAII-M and NSGAII-MC. ... Each experiment was executed 30 times for each PLA as recommended in [3] ... To analyze the results of the empirical study three different sets of solutions were used. ... In addition to these three sets of solutions, two quality indicators were used to evaluate the results. ... The most accepted indicator for performance assessment of multi-objective algorithms is the Hypervolume (HV) [32]. ... The second indicator, Euclidean Distance from the Ideal Solution (ED), is not a quality indicator, instead, it is used as a measure to help the decision maker in his/her ﬁnal decision, i.e., from all solutions provided which one should be selected.
spans.Hypotheses: We hypothesize that feature-driven crossover provides beneﬁts to PLA design.
spans.Parameters: We kicked off the parameters tuning using values adopted in related work [23], [29]. For instance, the generations number was set as 300 and the population size as 100. The mutation rate was empirically tuned as 0.9 since this rate outperformed other conﬁgurations (0.8, 1.0). The crossover rate was also empirically tuned for NSGAII-MC. The value 0.1 outperformed the other tested values: {0.2, 0.04}. It is important to highlight that in search-based design, mutation rates are high and crossover rates are low [25], [29].
spans.IndependentVariables: Arcade Game Maker (AGM) [28] ... Mobile Media (MM) [10] ... LPS-BET [13]
spans.DependentVariables: The most accepted indicator for performance assessment of multi-objective algorithms is the Hypervolume (HV) [32]. ... The second indicator, Euclidean Distance from the Ideal Solution (ED), is not a quality indicator, instead, it is used as a measure to help the decision maker in his/her ﬁnal decision, i.e., from all solutions provided which one should be selected.
spans.Procedure: Each experiment was executed 30 times for each PLA as recommended in [3], in order to reduce the possibility of the results were obtained by chance since search algorithms includes random variations. The number of ﬁtness evalua- tions was used as stop criterion. To analyze the results of the empirical study three different sets of solutions were used. The ﬁrst one is PFapprox. One set PFapprox for a PLA is obtained in each run of an algorithm. So, after 30 runs, 30 sets PFapprox were obtained. The second set is PFknown. This set was obtained for each PLA through the union of the 30 sets PFapprox, removing dominated and repeated solutions. PFknown represents the best solutions found by each algorithm. The last one is PFtrue. Since the actual PFtrue is not known, in our study this set was obtained for each PLA through the union of the sets PFknown, removing dominated and repeated solutions. PFtrue represents the best solutions known to the problem. This strategy to obtain the best solutions to a problem is recommended when the ideal set of solutions is not known [32].
spans.Summary: We introduced a feature-driven crossover operator that generates optimized designs from two different PLA designs by swapping groups of architectural elements realizing a particular feature. We implemented two versions of NSGAII: NSGAII-M using only mutation operators, and NSGAII-MC using mutation operators and the feature-driven crossover operator. We performed an empirical study applying NSGAII-M and NSGAII-MC for nine PLA designs aiming at comparing the obtained results. We hypothesize that feature-driven crossover provides beneﬁts to PLA design. The results of the conducted study corroborate to our hypothesis. Feature-driven crossover allows NSGAII ﬁnd better solution in terms of ﬁtness and higher diversity of solutions. A qualitative analysis showed the operator also provides solutions with higher quality in terms of feature-based cohesion and feature scattering and tangling.
spans.FutureWork: As future work, we intend to improve the feature-driven crossover to settle its limitations mentioned at the end of Section VII. Furthermore, we will investigate if a higher application rate to the feature-driven mutation operator provides PLA designs with higher feature modularization. We also intend to ask the opinion of the original PLA designers about the quality of obtained solutions. Thus, it will be possible to improve the feature-driven crossover encompassing drawbacks pointed by the designers.

spans.Background: Software product line (SPL) engineering is a software engineering approach to building conﬁgurable software systems. SPLs commonly use a feature model to capture and document the commonalities and variabilities of the underlying software system. A key challenge when using a feature model to derive a new SPL conﬁguration is determining how to ﬁnd an optimized feature selection that minimizes or maximizes an objective function, such as total cost, subject to resource constraints.
spans.Objective: To help address the challenges of optimizing feature selection in the face of resource constraints, this paper presents an approach that uses G enetic A lgorithms for optimized FE ature S election (GAFES) in SPLs.
spans.Methods: Thus we performed experiments based on the comparisons of GAFES with two techniques FCF + BBLP and FCF + M-HEU.
spans.Results: Our empirical results show that GAFES can produce solutions with 86–97% of the optimality of other automated feature selection algorithms and in 45–99% less time than existing exact and heuristic feature selection techniques.
spans.ProblemStatement: Open problem ⇒ SPL feature selection optimization with resource constraints. Despite the beneﬁts of SPLs, industrial case studies have shown that product derivation is still “a time-consuming and expensive activity” (Deelstra et al., 2004, 2005). Developers face a number of challenges when attempting to derive an optimized feature selection that meets an arbitrary set of requirements. For example, developers of the database SPL shown in Fig. 1 may need to derive the set of features that meets a set of functional requirements for a mobile application while simultaneously minimizing memory consumption (the optimization goal). Some conﬁgurations of the database may reduce memory consumption but require more disk space than can be supported by the mobile platform (a resource constraint).
spans.ResearchObjectives: Solution approach ⇒ genetic feature selection optimization algorithms. In this paper, we introduce an approach, based on genetic algorithms (GAs), to SPL feature selection optimization with resource constraints. A GA is a stochastic and global search heuristic that mimics natural evolution (Mitchell, 1996). GAs can quickly scan a vast population of possible solutions. These algorithms often work well for highly constrained problems, such as the Traveling Salesman (Muhlenbein, 1989) and satisﬁability problems (De Jong and Spears, 1989). Our approach, called Genetic Algorithms for optimized FEature Selection (GAFES), adapts GAs for SPL feature selection optimization with resource constraints. GAFES can quickly derive an optimized feature selection by evaluating different conﬁgurations that both optimize product capabilities and honor resource limitations. GAFES combines a novel feature selection repair operator and a penalty function for resource constraints to obtain fast feature selection times. Our empirical results show that GAFES can produce feature selections with objective function scores that are within 86–97% of the feature selections produced by prior feature selection techniques, such as FCF (White et al., 2009) and CSP/SAT-based approaches (Benavides et al., 2005; Batory, 2005; Czarnecki and Wasowski, 2007), for feature models whose size ranges from 10 to 10,000 features. Moreover, in our experiments, GAFES derives feature selections 45–99% faster than these existing heuristic and exact feature selection optimization techniques.
spans.Context: Software product lines (SPLs) are a software engineering approach for creating conﬁgurable software applications that can be adapted to a variety of requirement sets (Clements and Northrop, 2001). SPLs are built around a set of common software components with points of variability that allow for customization. For example, the Bold Stroke SPL (Boeing Company, 2002), developed by the Boeing company, comprises a wide range of reusable artifacts, such as a conﬁgurable architecture, set of application components, processes, and development tools, which are used to create Operational Flight Programs for a variety of Boeing aircraft.
spans.Goals: Thus we performed experiments based on the comparisons of GAFES with two techniques FCF + BBLP and FCF + M-HEU.
spans.ExperimentalUnits: GAFES ... FCF + BBLP and FCF + M-HEU.
spans.ExperimentalMaterial: We ﬁrst adopt Thum’s method (Thum et al., 2009) to randomly generate feature models with different characteristics (Section 7.1.1). For each feature model, an optimization problem instance with resource constraints is randomly generated (Section 7.1.2). Then we parametrically control the size of feature models and the percentage of cross-tree constraints respectively for a thorough runtime evaluation. ... All measurements were performed on the same Windows XP with Inter Pentium 4 CPU 3.0 GHz and 2 GB RAM. ... We used Thum et al.’s algorithm (Thum et al., 2009) to randomly generate feature models of size n. The algorithm operates as follows: starting with a single root node, the algorithm runs several iterations of the generation process. In each iteration, an existing feature without children is randomly selected, and between one and ten children are randomly added. These child features are connected to the parent either by And- (50% probability), Or- (25% probability) or Alternative-group (25% probability). Children in an And-group have a 50% probability of being optional. This iterative process is continued until the feature model has n features. All features with children are considered non-terminal. Moreover, we also generate cross-tree constraints (requires and excludes). For every k features, where k is based on the desired percentage of cross-tree constraints, one cross-tree constraint is generated. The cross-tree constraint is produced using the following algorithm: two different features are randomly selected, and then are connected randomly by either a requires (50% probability) or excludes (50% probability) link. According to Thum’s survey (Thum et al., 2009), these probabilities characterize the structure of the industrial feature models that they surveyed. The above generated feature models can be easily translated into propositional formulas (Batory, 2005; Thum et al., 2009). We used the SAT solver SAT4J 2 to validate these feature models and discarded all feature models that did not have any valid conﬁgurations (due to poorly chosen cross-tree constraints). We repeated the entire process until the appropriate number of valid feature models was generated.
spans.Hypotheses: Our hypothesis was that GAFES would be faster than FCF + BBLP because GAFES is an approximation algorithm and BBLP an exact one. GAFES would be also faster than FCF+M-HEU due to general knowledge of traditional GAs. In addition, we believed GAFES could obtain better optimality than the other two approaches. ... Based on the results of Experiment 1, our hypothesis for this experiment was that GAFES would be faster than FCF + M-HEU. But we expected GAFES to have slightly lower optimality than FCF + M-HEU. ... Our hypothesis was that the time consumption of the GAFES solutions would increase and the optimality would decrease as the percentage of cross-tree constraints increases.
spans.Parameters: In Experiments 1 (Section 7.2) and 2 (Section 7.3), we ﬁxed the following parameters: maximum number of children = 10, type of child group = (50%, 25%, 25%), optional child = 50%, number of cross-tree constraints = 0.1 × n, variables in cross-tree constrains = 2, and generated feature models with varying sizes. Again, Thum’s survey (Thum et al., 2009) shows that these parameters reﬂect real feature models. ... In Experiment 3 (Section 7.4), we ﬁxed the following parameters: total number of features n = 1000, maximum number of children = 10, type of child group = (50%, 25%, 25%), optional child = 50%, variables in cross-tree constrains = 2, and generated feature models with different percentage of cross-tree constraints from 0 to 30%. ... In order to create a feature selection optimization problem, values for the resource consumption and value of each feature must be generated. These values are created by generating pseudo-random numbers for the following problem parameters: (1) the resources consumed by each terminal feature r(tfi) = random(Rmax); (2) the resources consumed by each non-terminal feature r(nfi) = 0; (3) the value per unit resource that can be consumed by each terminal feature unitV = random(UnitVmax); (4) the value for each terminal feature v(tfi) = r(tfi) × unitV + random(Vmax); and (5) the value for each non-terminal feature v(nfi) = 0. Here, Rmax, UnitVmax, and Vmax are the upper bound on resource requirements, unit price of a resource, and the extra value of a feature after its consumed resource price. The value of each feature is not directly proportional to its resource consumption. The function random(i) returns an integer from 0 to (i − 1), following a uniform distribution. The total resources available for feature selections are then constrained to Rc = Rmax × nTF × 0.8 where nTF is the number of all terminal features in a feature model. ... For larger problems, we needed to generate problems for which we knew the optimal solution value. We used Akbar et al. (2001) test pattern generation technique to overcome this challenge. Akbar’s generation approach sets the problem parameters as follows: (1) a valid selection of terminal features is randomly chosen by the problem generator to serve as the optimal solution; (2) if S is the set of features randomly chosen to be in the optimal solution, then the generator sets R′(S) = R(S) = fi ∈ Sr(fi) so that the available resources exactly equal the resources needed for the optimal feature selection; and (3) the value associated with each of the randomly chosen optimal features is set to v′(fi) = r(fi) × unitV + Vmax. Thus V′(S) = fi ∈ Sv′(fi) = fi ∈ S(r(fi) × unitV + Vmax), which guarantees that there is no feature selection that ﬁts within the resource constraints and has a higher value than the feature selection that the problem generator selected to serve as the optimal solution.
spans.IndependentVariables: Independent variables in our experiments are the number of features in a feature model and the percentage of cross-tree constraints in a feature model.
spans.DependentVariables: The optimality and the time consumption of a solution are measured as dependent variables. ... Optimality is deﬁned as (Approximation Answer/Optimal Answer) to measure how close an algorithm can get to the optimal answer. Here, the Approximation Answer represents the total value of a solution produced by an approximation algorithm such as GAFES or FCF + M-HEU. Since BBLP is an exact technique, we use the total value of a solution produced by FCF + BBLP as the Optimal Answer. For example, for the same optimization problem (the same feature model, the same resource constraints, and the same optimization target), if GAFES obtains an approximate solution with the total value of 90 and FCF + BBLP obtains an optimal solution with the total value of 100, then the optimality of the GAFES solution is 90%. But ﬁnding exact solutions is NP-hard, which means that it is not feasible to apply FCF+BBLP to large feature models (e.g., number of features ≥ 500). Therefore, for large feature models (number of features ≥ 500), we used the test pattern generation technique devised by Akbar et al. (2001) to generate random optimization problem instances that we knew the optimal answer to (Section 7.1.2). The time consumption of a solution is measured by purely computing the running time of each algorithm (FCF + BBLP, FCF + M-HEU, and GAFES) to generate the solution. The startup time of the JVM and the time to generate the input feature model and the optimization problem instance are not considered. For example, the time consumption of a GAFES solution only comprises the running time of all steps described in Algorithm 1, i.e., the running time of population initialization and genetic iterations. Each genetic iteration is composed of chromosome selection, crossover, mutation, replacement, ﬁtness evaluation, and our repair operator called FesTransform. To guarantee precision, we used Java’s System.nanoTime() to capture the start and stop time of GAFES and the other algorithms. The scalability of each algorithm (FCF + BBLP, FCF + M-HEU, and GAFES) was evaluated by measuring how the time consumption of each algorithm increased as the feature models increased in size. Based on a statistical analysis of the time consumption of each algorithm to solve for feature selections on different size feature models, we evaluated and compared the scalability of the three algorithms. An algorithm was considered more scalable if the rate of increase in solving time as it was fed larger and larger feature models was lower than another algorithm.
spans.Procedure: To reduce the ﬂuctuations in dependent variables caused by random generation, we performed 100 repetitions for each conﬁguration of independent variables, i.e., we generated 100 random feature models with the same parameters and each performed the same algorithm for the same optimization problem. We only took the mean value of their results for analysis. ... We ﬁrst performed an experiment on small feature models with sizes n varying from 10 to 200. ... Here, the experiment was performed on each feature model whose size n varies from 10 to 200, as listed in the ﬁrst column. 100 feature models for each size were generated randomly with the same parameters, as described in Section 7.1.1, and we only took the mean value of their results. We only used the constants Rmax = 10, UnitVmax = 10, and Vmax = 20 for the generation of test cases, as explained in Section 7.1.2. We did not set a predeﬁned maximum of total value for any optimization problem instance. ... Hence, in this experiment, we only performed FCF + M-HEU and GAFES on large feature models whose size varies from 500 to 10,000. Moreover, due to the lack of the exact solutions, we adopted the test pattern generation technique described in Section 7.1.2 to obtain the optimal answer and the optimality achieved by the two heuristics (i.e., FCF + M-HEU and GAFES). ... Like Experiment 1, 100 feature models for each size were generated randomly with the same parameters, as described in Section 7.1.1, and we only took the mean value of their results. We still used the constants Rmax = 10, UnixVmax = 10, and Vmax = 20 for generation of test cases, as explained in Section 7.1.2. ... We measured the time consumption and the optimality of the GAFES solutions when ﬁxing the size of feature models to 1000 features and varying the percentage of cross-tree constraints in a feature model from 0 to 30%.
spans.Summary: To quickly derive an optimal product conﬁguration, developers need algorithmic techniques to automatically generate a valid feature selection that optimizes desired product properties. However, ﬁnding a feature selection with optimal product capability subject to required constraints is an NP-hard problem. Although there are numerous heuristic techniques for many NP-hard problems, they cannot directly support the SPL feature selection optimization with resource constraints because they are not designed to handle various structural and semantic constraints deﬁned in the feature model. This lack of heuristics limits the scale of feature model on which developers can realistically optimize and evaluate a large number of possible product conﬁgurations. This paper presents a GA-based optimized feature selection approach, GAFES, for automated product derivation in SPLs. A key component of GAFES is an algorithm that can transform an arbitrary feature selection into a valid feature combination conforming to the feature model constraints. Experiments show that GAFES can achieve an average of 86–90% optimality even for large feature models. Moreover GAFES can derive a feature selection 45–99% faster than existing heuristic and exact feature selection techniques. From our research on GAFES, we learned the following important lessons: 1. For large-scale feature models, exact techniques suffer from exponential algorithmic complexity and typically require days, months, or more, to solve large SPL feature selection optimization problems with resource constraints. In general, heuristic techniques have polynomial algorithmic complexity. GAFES is heuristic and is 45–97% faster than existing heuristics (e.g., FCF + M-HEU) for SPL feature selection problems. 2. GAFES produces solutions with 86–97% optimal of prior feature selection techniques. However, prior feature selection techniques, such as FCF+BBLP and FCF + M-HEU, obtain better optimality at the cost of longer solving time, which is caused by traversing a larger segment of the solution space. In addition, the optimality gained by GAFES maintains relatively stable for different size feature models. 3. GAFES is most applicable to domains, such as distributed real-time and embedded systems where the precise impact of feature selections on the performance and resource consumption of the product is known. 4. A key component of GAFES is the algorithm FesTransform that can, in most cases, transform an arbitrary feature selection (possibly invalid) into a valid feature combination in a feature model. Since many stochastic heuristics, such as GAs and ant colony optimization techniques, work on a range of randomly generated feature selections and ﬁnally generate an arbitrary feature selection, the algorithm FesTransform can be seen as a bridge for applying these stochastic heuristics to the SPL feature selection optimization problem.
spans.FutureWork: In future work, we plan to adapt more heuristics, such as ant colony optimization (Al-Ani, 2005) and particle swarm optimization (Lin et al., 2008), to the SPL feature selection optimization with resource constraints.

  "IndependentVariables": "Independent variables in our experiments are the number of features in a feature model and the percentage of cross-tree constraints in a feature model.",
  "DependentVariables": "The optimality and the time consumption of a solution are measured as dependent variables. ... Optimality is deﬁned as (Approximation Answer/Optimal Answer) to measure how close an algorithm can get to the optimal answer. Here, the Approximation Answer represents the total value of a solution produced by an approximation algorithm such as GAFES or FCF + M-HEU. Since BBLP is an exact technique, we use the total value of a solution produced by FCF + BBLP as the Optimal Answer. For example, for the same optimization problem (the same feature model, the same resource constraints, and the same optimization target), if GAFES obtains an approximate solution with the total value of 90 and FCF + BBLP obtains an optimal solution with the total value of 100, then the optimality of the GAFES solution is 90%. But ﬁnding exact solutions is NP-hard, which means that it is not feasible to apply FCF+BBLP to large feature models (e.g., number of features ≥ 500). Therefore, for large feature models (number of features ≥ 500), we used the test pattern generation technique devised by Akbar et al. (2001) to generate random optimization problem instances that we knew the optimal answer to (Section 7.1.2). The time consumption of a solution is measured by purely computing the running time of each algorithm (FCF + BBLP, FCF + M-HEU, and GAFES) to generate the solution. The startup time of the JVM and the time to generate the input feature model and the optimization problem instance are not considered. For example, the time consumption of a GAFES solution only comprises the running time of all steps described in Algorithm 1, i.e., the running time of population initialization and genetic iterations. Each genetic iteration is composed of chromosome selection, crossover, mutation, replacement, ﬁtness evaluation, and our repair operator called FesTransform. To guarantee precision, we used Java’s System.nanoTime() to capture the start and stop time of GAFES and the other algorithms. The scalability of each algorithm (FCF + BBLP, FCF + M-HEU, and GAFES) was evaluated by measuring how the time consumption of each algorithm increased as the feature models increased in size. Based on a statistical analysis of the time consumption of each algorithm to solve for feature selections on different size feature models, we evaluated and compared the scalability of the three algorithms. An algorithm was considered more scalable if the rate of increase in solving time as it was fed larger and larger feature models was lower than another algorithm.",
  "Procedure": "To reduce the ﬂuctuations in dependent variables caused by random generation, we performed 100 repetitions for each conﬁguration of independent variables, i.e., we generated 100 random feature models with the same parameters and each performed the same algorithm for the same optimization problem. We only took the mean value of their results for analysis. ... We ﬁrst performed an experiment on small feature models with sizes n varying from 10 to 200. ... Here, the experiment was performed on each feature model whose size n varies from 10 to 200, as listed in the ﬁrst column. 100 feature models for each size were generated randomly with the same parameters, as described in Section 7.1.1, and we only took the mean value of their results. We only used the constants Rmax = 10, UnitVmax = 10, and Vmax = 20 for the generation of test cases, as explained in Section 7.1.2. We did not set a predeﬁned maximum of total value for any optimization problem instance. ... Hence, in this experiment, we only performed FCF + M-HEU and GAFES on large feature models whose size varies from 500 to 10,000. Moreover, due to the lack of the exact solutions, we adopted the test pattern generation technique described in Section 7.1.2 to obtain the optimal answer and the optimality achieved by the two heuristics (i.e., FCF + M-HEU and GAFES). ... Like Experiment 1, 100 feature models for each size were generated randomly with the same parameters, as described in Section 7.1.1, and we only took the mean value of their results. We still used the constants Rmax = 10, UnixVmax = 10, and Vmax = 20 for generation of test cases, as explained in Section 7.1.2. ... We measured the time consumption and the optimality of the GAFES solutions when ﬁxing the size of feature models to 1000 features and varying the percentage of cross-tree constraints in a feature model from 0 to 30%.",
  "Summary": "To quickly derive an optimal product conﬁguration, developers need algorithmic techniques to automatically generate a valid feature selection that optimizes desired product properties. However, ﬁnding a feature selection with optimal product capability subject to required constraints is an NP-hard problem. Although there are numerous heuristic techniques for many NP-hard problems, they cannot directly support the SPL feature selection optimization with resource constraints because they are not designed to handle various structural and semantic constraints deﬁned in the feature model. This lack of heuristics limits the scale of feature model on which developers can realistically optimize and evaluate a large number of possible product conﬁgurations. This paper presents a GA-based optimized feature selection approach, GAFES, for automated product derivation in SPLs. A key component of GAFES is an algorithm that can transform an arbitrary feature selection into a valid feature combination conforming to the feature model constraints. Experiments show that GAFES can achieve an average of 86–90% optimality even for large feature models. Moreover GAFES can derive a feature selection 45–99% faster than existing heuristic and exact feature selection techniques. From our research on GAFES, we learned the following important lessons: 1. For large-scale feature models, exact techniques suffer from exponential algorithmic complexity and typically require days, months, or more, to solve large SPL feature selection optimization problems with resource constraints. In general, heuristic techniques have polynomial algorithmic complexity. GAFES is heuristic and is 45–97% faster than existing heuristics (e.g., FCF + M-HEU) for SPL feature selection problems. 2. GAFES produces solutions with 86–97% optimal of prior feature selection techniques. However, prior feature selection techniques, such as FCF+BBLP and FCF + M-HEU, obtain better optimality at the cost of longer solving time, which is caused by traversing a larger segment of the solution space. In addition, the optimality gained by GAFES maintains relatively stable for different size feature models. 3. GAFES is most applicable to domains, such as distributed real-time and embedded systems where the precise impact of feature selections on the performance and resource consumption of the product is known. 4. A key component of GAFES is the algorithm FesTransform that can, in most cases, transform an arbitrary feature selection (possibly invalid) into a valid feature combination in a feature model. Since many stochastic heuristics, such as GAs and ant colony optimization techniques, work on a range of randomly generated feature selections and ﬁnally generate an arbitrary feature selection, the algorithm FesTransform can be seen as a bridge for applying these stochastic heuristics to the SPL feature selection optimization problem.",
  "FutureWork": "In future work, we plan to adapt more heuristics, such as ant colony optimization (Al-Ani, 2005) and particle swarm optimization (Lin et al., 2008), to the SPL feature selection optimization with resource constraints."
}

spans.Background: Software product line (SPL) development is a new approach to software engineering which aims at the development of a whole range of products. However, as long as SPL can be useful, there are many challenges regarding the use of that approach. One of the main problems which hinders the adoption of software product line (SPL) is the complexity regarding product management. In that context, we can remark the scoping problem. One of the existent ways to deal with scoping is the product portfolio scoping (PPS). PPS aims to deﬁne the products that should be developed as well as their key features. In general, that approach is driven by marketing aspects, like cost of the product and customer satisfaction. Deﬁning a product portfolio by using the many different available aspects is a NP-hard problem.
spans.Objective: This work presents an improved hybrid approach to solve the feature model selection problem, aiming at supporting product portfolio scoping. The proposal is based in a hybrid approach not dependent on any particular algorithm/technology.
spans.Methods: We have evaluated the usefulness and scalability of our approach using one real SPL (ArgoUML-SPL) and synthetic SPLs.
spans.Results: As per the evaluation results, our approach is both useful from a practitioner’s perspective and scalable.
spans.ProblemStatement: A lot of attention has be given to the feature model selection problem (FMSP) [7,5], in which the objective is to select features and derive products from an SPL’s feature model, optimizing different objectives (e.g. proﬁtability), subjected to different types of restrictions (e.g. budget).
spans.ResearchObjectives: In our previous work [11], we presented an initial proposal to solve the feature model selection problem – and thus supporting PPS – by combining NSGA-II algorithm [12] with Mamdani fuzzy inference systems [13] (hybrid approach). The proposal in our previous work had three main drawbacks: (i) The previous proposal has a severe associated construct validity threat, which is due to the difﬁculty to obtain from SPLs the required data to run our approach; (ii) We only used a “toy” example to validate our approach and only class level correlation between features and assets was used; (iii) We did not conducted any statistical analysis of the results returned by the NSGA-II algorithm, as suggested by Arcuri and Briand [14]. Therefore, herein we put forward an extension of our previous work, which focused on improving the aforementioned issues.
spans.Context: A software product line (SPL) consists of a set of software products that share some core functionality – although differ in speciﬁc features – and are systematically developed using a collection of reusable assets [1–5]. A family of products associated with an SPL is described by a feature model, which deﬁnes the constraints between features (system functionality) and the valid products.
spans.Goals: • RQ2 – What is the usefulness of the improved hybrid approach in the real word? • RQ3 – How scalable is the improved hybrid approach?
spans.ExperimentalUnits: our approach with a random search algorithm.
spans.ExperimentalMaterial: All the experiments were performed using a laptop with Intel(R) Core(TM)i5-3230M Quad Core 2.60 GHz processor and 8 GB of RAM. We have used jMetal API to implement NSGA-II in our approach [53] and the fuzzy inference systems were implemented using JFuzzyLogic API [52]. ... To evaluate the usefulness of our approach in the real word, we used ArgoUML-SPL,3 which is an SPL extracted from a widely adopted UML modeling tool called ArgoUML.4 We selected this SPL because it is very often used in SPL-related studies. This SPL has 120,000 lines of code and 9 features. Fig. 3 displays ArgoUML-SPL’s feature model.5 ArgoUML-SPL has 9 features and there is no semantical dependency relationship between its features, i.e. any optional feature selection is considered as valid. Note that there is only one mandatory feature (Class Diagram). The product portfolio for ArgoUML-SPL that was composed using our approach addresses two different customers’ segment: agile software developers (agile segment) and plan-driven software developers (traditional segment). The ArgoUML-SPL has eight features, which represent its functional and non-functional requirements [56]. The LOGGING feature is responsible for registering events related to exceptions and information used to help the debugging activity. Six other features are related to each UML diagram available in the tool (Activity Diagram, State Diagram, Sequence Diagram, Use Cases Diagram, Collaboration Diagram and Deployment Diagram). Finally, it has the cognitive support feature, which is responsible helping developers with the detection of problems in their projects. ... To evaluate the scalability of our approach, we created a synthetic SPL based on ArgoUML-SPL.
spans.Parameters: The NSGA-II algorithm was executed 1000 times for each customers’ segment in both evaluations, to reduce the impact of its stochastic nature. We used a predeﬁned number of iteration (6) as the termination criterion. The size of the populations P, crossover (two-point operator) C and mutation (bit-ﬂip operator) rate R were respectively equal to 30, 0.9 and 0.05. We used the binary tournament selection operator. ... To use fuzzy inference systems, it is necessary to map the knowledge of domain experts in terms of fuzzy sets and a production rules’ base. Herein, we used our own knowledge together to conﬁgure the rules’ bases associated with the fuzzy inference system in stage 1. We conﬁgured stage 4 using values obtained through interviews with practitioners from both customers’ segments that use the ArgoUML tool: • Agile – We interviewed (unstructured interviews) three project managers of Infoway,1 which is a software development company that has been applying agile software development practices for over 10 years. • Traditional – We interviewed three project managers of Synergia,2 which is an institution from the Brazilian public sector that develops software for both the private and public sectors. They have used an UP-like (Uniﬁed Process) software process [54] for 8 years. We deﬁned the fuzzy sets associated with the input and output variables in an empirical way, i.e. we adjusted the fuzzy sets parameters to ensure that the output values would comply with the knowledge of the experts together with our own knowledge. In both fuzzy systems, we used ﬁve fuzzy sets to map the domain knowledge associated with their respective output variables (cost in stage 1 and suitability in stage 4), which are represented by the linguistic variables Very Low (VL), Low (L), Medium (M), High (H) and Very High (VH). The knowledge associated with the input variables in both fuzzy systems were mapped into three fuzzy sets, which are represented by the linguistic variables Low (L), Medium (M), High (H). All the fuzzy sets were deﬁned using triangular membership functions. The rules’ base used in the stage-1 fuzzy system is displayed in Table 1, while the one associated with the stage-4 fuzzy system is presented in Table 2. Note that in both inference systems the input and output variables were normalized inside the domain of a real scale from 0 to 10.
spans.IndependentVariables: our approach with a random search algorithm.
spans.DependentVariables: We have used three performance metrics to analyze the results of the evaluation. Hyper volume (HV) [55] is a very popular metric due to its good theoretical and practical properties, such as being compliant with Pareto dominance – if one population Pareto dominates another then it has a higher HV – and not requiring the problem’s Pareto front to be known. HV calculates the volume of the objective space between the obtained solution set and a reference point. A large value is preferable and reﬂects good performance of the solution set in terms of convergence, extensity and uniformity. We have also used the suitability of the ﬁnal product as a metric. As aforementioned, this value is obtained through the analysis of several aspects of a product, including the opinion of the customers and the cost of the feature as per developers’ opinion. This is an innovation of this proposal and a metric to be compared among the several algorithms that may be inserted in the optimization phase of the approach. Finally, we have used the time spent to ﬁnd the suggested products as metric too.
spans.Procedure: In three of the ﬁve stages of our approach, we employ computational intelligence techniques, which require some parametrization. In addition, to analyze the results produced through the execution of metaheuristics (NSGA-II in stage 3 of our approach), it is mandatory to use some performance metrics. ... To evaluate the scalability of our approach, we created a synthetic SPL based on ArgoUML-SPL. To do so, we carried out the following process: 1. We randomly generated 1000 data points following a normal distribution that has the same mean and standard deviation of the ArgoUML-SPL features’ cost. 2. We also randomly generated 1000 data points following a normal distribution that has the same mean and standard deviation of the ArgoUML-SPL features’ relevance. 3. We created the synthetic SPL, which has 1000 features, by combining the data points created in steps 1 and 2. The data points were randomly combined to generate 1000 unique pairs. Like ArgoUML-SPL, the synthetic SPL has just one mandatory feature. Note that its features have only cost and relevance as attributes. We did so to simplify the creation of the synthetic SPL.7
spans.Summary: In this paper we proposed an improved hybrid approach to solve the feature model selection problem, aiming at supporting product portfolio scoping. The proposal put forward herein improved our previous work [11] by making our hybrid approach independent of any particular algorithm/technology and by developing two tools that improves the collection of required input (RQ1). We also evaluate the usefulness and scalability of our approach using one real SLP (ArgoUML-SPL) and one synthetic SPL. As per the evaluation results, our approach is both useful from a practitioner’s perspective (RQ2) and scalable (RQ3). To make our results and conclusions more reliable, we followed the guidelines by Arcuri and Briand [14]. We also performed a sanity check contrasting the results of our approach with a random search algorithm. The results show that our approach performs better than an ordinary random search algorithm. Finally, we calculated the hypervolume for the results and the results are reasonable as per existing literature [60].
spans.FutureWork: We intend to further evaluate the approach improved in this paper using a more diverse set of SPLs, accounting for different domains with different customers segments.
