spans.Background: Feature models are commonly used to capture and communicate the commonality and variability of features in a Software Product Line. The core component of Feature models is feature diagrams, which graphically depict features in a hierarchical form. In previous work we have proposed a new notation that aims to improve the cognitive effectiveness of feature diagrams.
spans.Objective: The objective of this paper is to empirically validate the cognitive effectiveness of the new feature diagrams notation in comparison to its original form.
spans.Methods: We use two distinct empirical user-studies to validate the new notation. The ﬁrst empirical study uses the survey approach while the second study is a subject-based experiment. The survey study investigates the semantic transparency of the new notation while the second study investigates the speed and accuracy of reading the notation.
spans.Results: The results of the studies indicate that the proposed changes have signiﬁcantly improved its cognitive effectiveness,
spans.Conclusions: The cognitive effectiveness of feature diagrams has been improved, however there remains fur- ther research for full acceptance of the new notation by its potential user community.
spans.ProblemStatement: However, evaluating and improving the cognitive effectiveness of feature diagrams have little attention from the research commu- nity, which is arguably equally as important to consider and research. In summary, many research works focused on enabling the modeler, but few have focused on enabling the model reader. The most likely reason that this important stream of research has been neglected is the lack of a theoretical basis to conduct notation evaluations [36].
spans.ResearchObjectives: In this paper we provide a more comprehensive evaluation and presentation of the original notation and the proposed notation.
spans.Context: Software product line engineering is emerging as an effective de- velopment paradigm that enables ﬂexible response and mass cus- tomization [45]. Software product line engineering considers all de- velopment aspects for producing a set of related products that share more commonalities than variations [5]. Software product lines al- low for mass customization, which is deﬁned by Tseng and Jiao [59] as “producing goods and services to meet individual customer’s needs with near mass production eﬃciency”, in mass production environ- ments [5]. Traditional mass production lines no longer suﬃce mar- ket needs and hence mass customization becomes a critical factor for development success [45].
spans.Goals: The aim of this experiment is to determine whether the newly proposed feature diagram notation can be used to develop diagrams that can be syntactically read more effectively than diagrams devel- oped using the original notation.
spans.ExperimentalUnits: The educational experience of all the students involved in the experiment is similar and can be determined. The experiment took place during the Winter 2014 semester. At the time of conducting the experiment, the students have already completed three program- ming courses in addition to an introductory Software Engineering course that covers the subject of feature diagrams and software prod- uct lines. It is beneﬁcial that the subjects were familiar with feature diagrams as this helped signiﬁcantly reduce their learning curve in preparation for the experiment. There were a total of 31 students in- volved in the experiment. The students were divided randomly into two groups (Group A = 15 students, Group B = 16 students). The most important goal of the subject selection phase is to construct groups whom relative abilities are approximate so that their ability levels do not inﬂuence the results obtained. Success of this task can only be proven by performing statistical analysis that show that the relative ability levels of the subjects in the groups did not affect the results of the experiment. This analysis is shown in Section 7.9.1.4. The subjects were given three lectures that covered the subject of software product lines and feature diagrams. In a subsequent lab ses- sion, the subjects performed exercises that further strengthen their knowledge of the feature diagrams notation. The ﬁnal session intro- duced the subjects to the newly proposed notation. The ﬁnal session also required the subject to perform some exercises in order to famil- iarize themselves with the new notation.
spans.ExperimentalMaterial: We developed a simple software tool that the subjects will use to perform the experimental tasks. The experiment took place in the same laboratory to ensure that they did not use different screen sizes which may potentially inﬂuence their performance. The tool was de- signed to present the subjects with one feature diagram at a time which would be ﬁxed on the left-hand side of the screen while the questions were shown on the right-hand side. The tool was also de- signed to present only one question at a time. The order of the ques- tions was randomized for each diagram in order to mitigate learning effects. The tool recorded the response times and errors committed.
spans.Tasks: A 2 × 2 partial factorial design with repeated measures was used. This experiment was used in order to mitigate the effect of individual and group abilities. All subjects were required to consider two feature diagrams. The ﬁrst diagram presents features similar to those present in the popular document processing software Adobe [1]. The second diagram presents features from the ERP (Enterprise Resource Plan- ning) business management software deployed at King Fahd Univer- sity. For ease of reference, the two diagrams used will be referred to as the PDF (Portable Document Format) and ERP diagrams from this point onwards. The PDF and ERP diagrams are shown in Appendix A, respectively. The syntax related questions are presented in Appendix C. The feature diagrams were not directly reverse engineered from the sources and they do not resemble the actual systems they repre- sent. The as-is “real” diagrams could not be used as they do not satisfy a number of criteria. Instead the diagrams were designed to remain realistic while satisfying the following criteria: ... The diagrams used need to be large to reduce external validity. For this criterion we referred to other similar empirical studies re- lated to model comprehension for benchmarking purposes, such as the studies presented in Gopalakrishnan et al. [22]; Purchase et al. [48]; Reijers and Mendling [50]. The diagrams used in this experiment were approximately twice the size of the diagrams used in Gopalakrishnan et al. [22]; Purchase et al. [48]; Reijers and Mendling [50]. ... Both versions of each diagram (using the new and original no- tations) diagram were developed using an identical layout. This criterion is important as empirical evidence related to notation understandability has shown that diagrammatic layout features have an effect on graph comprehension [47].
spans.Hypotheses: For the response times variable (T), the alternative hypothesis in- dicates that feature diagrams built using the new notation will be read quicker than feature diagrams developed using the original no- tation. For the errors committed variable (E), the alternative hypoth- esis states that subjects will commit fewer errors when answering questions about feature diagrams developed using the new notation than diagrams developed using the original notation. Both hypothe- ses are set as one-tailed (Table 6) ... Null hypothesis (Ho): (Ho1): T (NN) = T (ON), (Ho2): E (NN) = E (ON) ... Alternative hypothesis (Ha): T (NN) < T (ON), (Ha2): E (NN) < E (ON)
spans.IndependentVariables: The experiment has two treatments: (a) the use of the original notation (ON) and, (b) the use of the new nota- tion (NN).
spans.DependentVariables: The ﬁrst variable pertains to the speed of reading and it is a measure of the response times (T) for subjects to answer questions related to one diagram type. The second variable represents the errors commit- ted (E) when answering questions related to one diagram type.
spans.Procedure: The subjects were provided with two diagrams to consider, one di- agram at a time. Each subject was provided one diagram constructed using the new notation and another diagram constructed using the original notation. The subjects were provided a questionnaire con- taining questions related only to the diagrammatic constructs of the diagrams. The questionnaire contains two identical sets of questions, one set for each diagram. The legends of both notations printed in color on a single sheet of paper. The response times and the answers to the questionnaires were measured using a tool support. The sub- jects were informed that they were allowed only one session to com- plete the experimental tasks. However, they were informed that there is no time limit to perform the tasks as to not feel timing pressures. A post-experiment questionnaire contained a question that speciﬁ- cally veriﬁes from the students that they indeed not feel timing pres- sures. The post-experiment questionnaire also contained questions pertaining to the notations they used. These questions provide im- portant qualitative data that can help explain the quantitative results. In particular, the post-experiment questionnaire contained three im- portant questions. The ﬁrst question asks the subject which notation they preferred. The second question asks the subject why they pre- ferred the notation they selected and which speciﬁc aspects about it that they liked the most. The third question asks the subject about the various changes that they feel will further improve the notation they selected. Time used to answer qualitative questions was not recorded.
spans.AnalysisProcedure: The quantitative data related to response times and errors com- mitted were considered as discrete data. Errors committed were con- sidered as discrete data since there is no evidence that will allow us to safely assign unequal unit weightings to the different types of errors. We used the Shapiro–Wilk test to examine if the data sets complied with the normality assumptions [55]. For this experiment, we used the Shapiro–Wilk test as it does not require that the mean or variance of the hypothesized normal distribution to be speciﬁed in advance. Another reason for using the Shapiro–Wilk test is that there was no causal explanation as to the nature of the distribution that the data points are sampled from. Data sets were then compared to detect sta- tistically signiﬁcant results using the Mann–Whitney U statistic [56]. The Hodges–Lehman method was used to calculate the conﬁdence in- tervals around the difference between medians given at the standard p<0.05 level [32]. Tool support was used to record response time and to perform the scoring of the answers. Time and scoring were performed automati- cally using tool support. Qualitative data was stored in a spreadsheet.
spans.Summary: This paper presented an evaluation of the visual syntax of fea- ture diagrams based on the PoN principles. The evaluation revealed a number of drawbacks in the notational set of feature diagrams. Con- sequently, a set of symbol modiﬁcations were proposed in order to remedy some of the identiﬁed drawbacks and improve the overall cognitive effectiveness of feature diagrams. The proposed improve- ments were also based on the PoN principles. The proposed improve- ments were empirical validated using two user studies. The ﬁrst user study is performed using a survey that validates the semantic trans- parency of the proposed symbols. The participants of the survey were limited software engineering professionals and academic. The second user study is performed as an experiment and it involved software engineering students. The experiment evaluated the overall cognitive effectiveness of the proposed notation by using the original notation as a benchmark. The experiment set two hypotheses; one related to the response times and the other related errors committed. The main ﬁnding of the experiment is that the new notation can be read signif- icantly quicker than the original notation while committing signiﬁ- cantly fewer reading errors. Qualitative data obtained indicates that the subjects did not face fatigue, maturation or time pressure. Therefore, we believe that the results obtained in this experiment are solely inﬂuenced by the use of the different notations. Moreover, according to the qualitative data obtained, the subjects generally preferred the new feature diagrams notation over the original notation. The subjects indicated that the main reason for their preference of the new notation was the use of colors, especially the changes applied to the relationship symbols. In- cidentally, subjects who criticized the new notation cited their main reason for their criticism is its extensive use of colors and resulting accessibility concerns. Ultimately, notation design is always open to improvements. Since notations are used by human beings, then nat- urally there will never be one design that is deemed perfect by all users. Therefore, the success criterion of this research work is to cre- ate a notation that is at least more cognitively effective than the origi- nal notation. The empirical data obtained validates the success of this research work. The research work and the results presented in this paper, al- though favorable, can by no means be considered as the ﬁnal stage of proving the superiority of the new notation in comparison to the original; far from it actually. Our view of the results obtained is con- servative. The need for this conservatism is mainly due to the fact that the PoN deﬁnes principles at the symbol level, not at the diagram- level. This means that while the cognitive effectiveness of the build- ing blocks (symbols) of models have improved, there is no evidence that cognitive effectiveness at the diagram level has also improved. A symbol may be more cognitively effective than its counterpart, how- ever if this symbol is used many times in a large diagram, then it may actually reduce the cognitive effectiveness of the entire diagram in comparison to when the original notation is used. One obvious is- sue with our new notation is that it is not as spatially economical as the original notation. Our new notation leads to more cluttering, an obviously undesired side-effect. The PoN encourages the use of color, but gives no guidance on how many colors should be used or what color combinations are allowed. The main reason why our new notation did not follow principles set forth by a theory that speciﬁ- cally considers cognitive effectiveness at the diagram-level is that no such developed theory was available (as is the PoN at the symbol- level). The literature provides many useful pieces of knowledge with this respect, but such dispersed knowledge needs to be compiled and theorized as a set of principles (much like PoN) that is readily avail- able for notation designers to use. The lack of such theoretical basis at the diagram-level is the main reason our empirical studies focused mainly at the symbol-level. Although it is not diﬃcult to conjure and prescribe diagram-level tasks for our subjects and measure the ef- fects of our new notation at that level, the fact would remain that such effects (positive or negative) would merely be stumbled upon by chance. In fact, the lack of a theoretical basis at the diagram-level would render all our design decisions (which we did not consciously make) at the diagram level as arbitrary.
spans.FutureWork: Our future work is currently being directed towards researching the literature in order to theorize cognitive effectiveness at the diagram-level and creating a new set of principles for this purpose (perhaps to be called the “Physics of Di- agrams”). At this stage, the results obtained from these studies can only be considered preliminary. Based on the empirical evidence obtained, future work can be direct towards availing automation support, which will greatly aid its adoption by potential users. Tool support can be easily made available by changing variable values that relate to symbol graph- ics in existing tools. For example, a given symbol can be encoded to have “symbol.color = BLACK;” can be then changed to “symbol.color = RED”. Moreover, a number of pictorial ﬁles will be needed in order depict icons. Encouraged by the results of this research, we plan to direct our future work towards conduct- ing evaluations of other Software Engineering notations. For example, the visual syntax of SysML (“SysML.org: SysML Speciﬁcations,” 2014), KAOS [15] and TROPOS [9] diagrams can be evaluated and improved. The evaluations and proposed improvements should be based on the PoN and empirically validated using a similar framework as shown in this paper. We also plan to direct future research towards con- ducting a systematic literature review that investigates the subject of cognitive effectiveness in modeling to provide a comprehensive literature base that can be used to guide future research in the area. Another use of tool support can be directed towards aiding the evaluation of existing notations and evaluating the suggested im- provements as well. Tool support can also be used to create another dialect of the new notation that better caters to the colorblind com- munity. For example, a tool can render the colored symbols using dif- ferent pattern ﬁlls instead of colors. It should be noted that we do not intend for our new notation to replace the original outright. If for any reason users of feature dia- grams ﬁnd it more better to use the original notation then they are certainly encouraged to do so, even if the sole reason is due to per- sonal taste (after all this research ﬁeld deals with human aspects and their various preferences should be observed). We intend for our no- tation to be an alternative to the original notation. There may be many situations where our new notation can be considered better, espe- cially given the ubiquity of High-Deﬁnition computer screens, tablets, smartphones and colored printers.

spans.Background:
The software product line (PL) architecture (PLA)
is one of the most important PL core assets as it is the
abstraction of the products that can be generated, and it
represents similarities and variabilities of a PL. Its quality
attributes analysis and evaluation can serve as a basis for
analyzing the managerial and economical values of a PL.
spans.Objective:
We proposed metrics for PLA complexity and extensibility
quality attributes.
spans.Methods:
This paper is concerned with the empirical
validation of such metrics.
spans.Conclusions:
As a result of the experimental
work we can conclude that the metrics are relevant indicators
of complexity and extensibility of PLA by presenting their
correlation analysis.
spans.ProblemStatement:
The evaluation of a PLA must be supported by a set of
metrics [7]. Such metrics must both evidence the quality
of PL and serve as a basis to analyze the managerial and
economical value of a PL [2]. The PLA must explicit the
common (similarities) and variable (variabilities) aspects of
a PL. The variability impact analysis on the PL develop-
ment can determine the aggregated value of a PL for an
organization. Metrics for a PLA are applied to a set of assets
from which variants can be generated rather than one speciﬁc
product. Thus, it is necessary to deﬁne speciﬁc PLA metrics
to provide effective indicators with regard to the overall PL
development and evolution.
spans.ResearchObjectives:
This paper is concerned with the empirical validation of
the proposed metrics for PLA complexity and extensibility
quality attributes. The validation aims at correlating the
metrics CompPLA and ExtensPLA with subject’s complexity
and extensibility rating, respectively, when generating PLA
conﬁgurations. A PLA conﬁguration represents a derived PL
product with variabilities resolved.
spans.Context:
In the last decades effective methodologies to evaluate
software architectures, such as ATAM (Architecture Trade-
off Analysis Method) and SAAM (Software Architecture
Analysis Method), were proposed and consolidated by both
industrial and academic segments [6]. Such a consolidation
is corroborated by the analysis of the number of published
research papers and technical reports providing important
examples of how to carry out a software architecture evalu-
ation based on quality attributes. Thus, these methodologies
are essential for evaluating single-product architectures.
spans.Goals:
Analyze collected metrics from UML models and source
code
For the purpose of validating
With respect to the capability to be used as PLA com-
plexity and extensibility indicators
From the point of view of software product line archi-
tects
In the context of graduate students and lecturers of the
Software Engineering area at the University of Waterloo
(UWaterloo), University of S˜ao Paulo (ICMC-USP), and
State University of Maring´a (UEM)
spans.ExperimentalUnits:
The six subjects were: one
Master student and one PhD candidate from ICMC-USP,
one lecturer from UEM, one Master student and two PhD
candidates from UWaterloo. They have at least minimal
experience in the design of product lines and variabilities
using UML.
spans.ExperimentalMaterial:
The objects were: a document descri-
bing the Arcade Game Maker (AGM) PL [12]; AGM UML
class and component models, a traceability model from
classes to components; and a resolution model containing
the variabilities to be resolved at class level. In addition,
each subject received a copy of the experiment’s Terms of
Agreement and a questionnaire to answer. The independent
variables were measured by the proposed metrics. The
dependent variables were measured according to the subjects
ratings of complexity and extensibility.
spans.Tasks:
The six subjects were given the material described in
Preparation (Section II-C1). It was required to each subject
to generate ﬁve AGM conﬁgurations. It was done by following
instructions on how to resolve the AGM variability resolution
model, and how to rate the complexity and extensibility
associated to the conﬁgurations generated from the subjects
view point. All the tasks were performed by each subject
alone, with no time limit to solve them.
spans.Hypotheses:
The following hypothesis
were tested in this study:
• Null Hypothesis (H0): There is no signiﬁcant correla-
tion between the PLA complexity metric (CompPLA)
and the subject’s complexity rating for each PLA con-
ﬁguration, and neither between the PLA extensibility
metric (ExtensPLA) and the subject’s extensibility ra-
ting for each PLA conﬁguration;
• Alternative Hypothesis (H1): There is a signiﬁcant
correlation between the PLA complexity metric (Comp-
PLA) and the subject’s complexity rating for each PLA
conﬁguration, but there is no signiﬁcant correlation be-
tween the PLA extensibility metric (ExtensPLA) and the
subjects extensibility rating for each PLA conﬁguration;
• Alternative Hypothesis (H2): There is a signiﬁcant
correlation between the PLA extensibility metric (Ex-
tensPLA) and the subject’s extensibility rating for each
PLA conﬁguration, but there is no signiﬁcant correla-
tion between the PLA complexity metric (CompPLA)
and the subjects complexity rating for each PLA con-
ﬁguration; and
• Alternative Hypothesis (H3): There is a signiﬁcant
correlation between both the PLA complexity metric
(CompPLA) and the subjects complexity rating, and the
PLA extensibility metric (ExtensPLA) and the subjects
extensibility rating.
spans.IndependentVariables:
The independent variables were
the class and component complexity and extensibility of
a PLA.
spans.DependentVariables:
The dependent variables were the complexity and
extensibility of each product generated from the PLA.
spans.Procedure:
The six subjects were given the material described in
Preparation (Section II-C1). It was required to each subject
to generate ﬁve AGM conﬁgurations. It was done by following
instructions on how to resolve the AGM variability resolution
model, and how to rate the complexity and extensibility
associated to the conﬁgurations generated from the subjects
view point. All the tasks were performed by each subject
alone, with no time limit to solve them. All
the data was collected including the subjects rating obtained
from the responses of the questionnaire and the metric values
were calculated manually.
spans.Summary:
Current literature claims the need of metrics to allow PL
architects empirically analyze the potential of a PLA, as
well as PL managers analyze the aggregated managerial and
economical values of a PL throughout its products.
Performing empirical validation of metrics is essential to
demonstrate their practical usefulness. The proposed metrics
for complexity (CompPLA) and extensibility (ExtensPLA)
PLA quality attributes were empirically validated based on
their application to a set of 30 products generated by experi-
ment subjects from the Arcade Game Maker (AGM) PL. The
observed metric values were submitted to normality tests
which proved their non-normality. Then, Spearman’s rank
correlation was used to demonstrate the metrics correlations,
which are:
• CompPLA has a strong positive correlation with the
subjects complexity rating;
• ExtensPLA has a strong positive correlation with the
subjects extensibility rating;
• CompPLA and ExtensPLA have a strong positive cor-
relation with each other.
Linear regression was used to come up with equations that
express the correlation between the metrics and the subjects
rating, as well as the metrics themselves.
Although we have used a non-commercial PL to conduct
our experiments, we had evidences that our proposed me-
trics can be used as relevant indicators of complexity and
extensibility of a PLA based on its derived products.
spans.FutureWork:
We are currently proposing some changes on various
issues to improve our experiments with metrics, which are:
• increase the derived conﬁgurations sample size, which
is important to stay closer to real projects and to
generalize the results;
• conduct experiments in a more controlled environment;
• deal with real data from commercial PL obtained from
industrial environments; and
• recruit more subjects from the Software Engineering
area, both from academic and industrial environments.

extensibility of each product generated from the PLA.",
  "Procedure": "The six subjects were given the material described in
Preparation (Section II-C1). It was required to each subject
to generate ﬁve AGM conﬁgurations. It was done by following
instructions on how to resolve the AGM variability resolution
model, and how to rate the complexity and extensibility
associated to the conﬁgurations generated from the subjects
view point. All the tasks were performed by each subject
alone, with no time limit to solve them. All
the data was collected including the subjects rating obtained
from the responses of the questionnaire and the metric values
were calculated manually.",
  "Summary": "Current literature claims the need of metrics to allow PL
architects empirically analyze the potential of a PLA, as
well as PL managers analyze the aggregated managerial and
economical values of a PL throughout its products.
Performing empirical validation of metrics is essential to
demonstrate their practical usefulness. The proposed metrics
for complexity (CompPLA) and extensibility (ExtensPLA)
PLA quality attributes were empirically validated based on
their application to a set of 30 products generated by experi-
ment subjects from the Arcade Game Maker (AGM) PL. The
observed metric values were submitted to normality tests
which proved their non-normality. Then, Spearman’s rank
correlation was used to demonstrate the metrics correlations,
which are:
• CompPLA has a strong positive correlation with the
subjects complexity rating;
• ExtensPLA has a strong positive correlation with the
subjects extensibility rating;
• CompPLA and ExtensPLA have a strong positive cor-
relation with each other.
Linear regression was used to come up with equations that
express the correlation between the metrics and the subjects
rating, as well as the metrics themselves.
Although we have used a non-commercial PL to conduct
our experiments, we had evidences that our proposed me-
trics can be used as relevant indicators of complexity and
extensibility of a PLA based on its derived products.",
  "FutureWork": "We are currently proposing some changes on various
issues to improve our experiments with metrics, which are:
• increase the derived conﬁgurations sample size, which
is important to stay closer to real projects and to
generalize the results;
• conduct experiments in a more controlled environment;
• deal with real data from commercial PL obtained from
industrial environments; and
• recruit more subjects from the Software Engineering
area, both from academic and industrial environments."
}

spans.Background: The existing UML-based variability management approaches in the literature, including SMarty, do not provide empirical evidence of their effectiveness, which is an essential requirement for technology transfer to industry.
spans.Objective: Therefore, this paper presents empirical evidence of the SMarty approach at class level.
spans.Methods: This study is characterized as a quasi-experiment [17]
spans.Conclusions: In addition, this paper demonstrates how SMarty has evolved, by means of its proﬁle and guidelines, based on the obtained results of an experiment and the subjects feedback analysis.
spans.ProblemStatement: Although the several variability management approaches existing in the literature, there is a lack of empirical evaluation of these approaches, in relation to their effectiveness, allowing them to be transferred and adopted by industry [7].
spans.ResearchObjectives: This paper aims to evaluate the effectiveness of the SMarty approach with regard to the PLUS method, for the purpose of empirically identify issues on class models with modeled variabilities and therefore contributing to SMarty by means of its proﬁle and respective guidelines for variabilities.
spans.Context: Amongst existing variability management approaches there are SMarty [5] and the PLUS method [6]. SMarty aims to manage variabilities in UML models supported by a proﬁle and a set of guidelines for applying such a proﬁle to use case, class, component, activity and sequence models. PLUS is a well-known method that allows explicit modeling of common and variable features supported by stereotypes for use cases and classes.
spans.Goals: The goal of the experiment was to compare the PLUS method and the SMarty approach, for the purpose of identify the most effective, with respect to the capability of identiﬁ- cation and representation of variabilities in Software Product Line class models, from the point of view of software product line architects, in the context of master and Ph.D. students of the Software Engineering area from the University of S˜ao Paulo (ICMC/USP) and Federal University of S˜ao Carlos (UFSCar).
spans.ExperimentalUnits: the subjects must be gradu- ate students, lecturers or practitioners of the software engineering area with at least minimal knowledge in modeling classes. The knowledge in modeling class by each subject will be obtain based on the characteriza- tion questionnaire, where the subject indicates, besides their experience in UML, the knowledge in SPL and variability concepts. In addition, after the training sessions, each subject must be familiar with the essential variability management concepts (Section II-A).
spans.ExperimentalMaterial: every subject was giving the follow- ing documents: • the consent term to the experimental study; • a characterization questionnaire, in which the sub- jects must indicate their academic background, area of expertise and experience, their level of experience with the UML notation and the SPL approach; and • the description of the e-commerce and AGM SPLs and their class models with no variabilities repre- sented.
spans.Tasks: The main task for each subject was reading and under- standing the e-commerce and Arcade Game Maker SPLs overviews. Then, the subjects annotated variabilities in the e-commerce and Arcade Game Maker class models.
spans.Hypotheses: the following hypotheses were tested in this study: • Null Hypothesis (H0): both X and Y approaches are equally effective in terms of representing vari- abilities in class models. H0 : μ(effectiveness(X)) = μ(effectiveness(Y)); • Alternative Hypothesis (H1): X approach is less effective than Y approach. H1 : μ(effectiveness(X)) < μ(effectiveness(Y)); and • Alternative Hypothesis (H2): X approach is more effective than Y approach. H2 : μ(effectiveness(X)) > μ(effectiveness(Y)).
spans.IndependentVariables: Independent Variables: • the variability management approach, which is a factor with two treatments: X and Y; and • the SPL, which is a factor with two treatments: e- commerce and AGM.
spans.DependentVariables: Dependent Variables: the effectiveness, based on the studies from Martiinez-Ruiz et al. [20], C¸ ¨oteli [21] and Basili and Selby [22], was calculated for each variability management approach (X and Y) as follows: effectiveness(z) = nV arC −nV arI where: • z is a given variability management approach • nVarC is the number of correct identiﬁed and mod- eled variability elements according to the z approach • nVarI is the number of incorrect identiﬁed and modeled variability elements according to the z approach A variability element might be either a variation point or a variant.
spans.Procedure: Participation procedure: standard procedures were adopted for each subject participation, which are: a) the subject came along the place where the study was conducted; b) the experimenter gives the subject a set of docu- ments: the experimental study consent term; the characterization questionnaire; essential concepts on variability management in SPL; and the descrip- tion of the e-commerce and Arcade Game Maker SPLs. c) the subject reads each given document; d) the experimenter explains the given documents; e) the experimenter randomly associates each subject to the X or Y approach; f) the experimenter trains the subjects on the respec- tive approach; g) the subject reads and clariﬁes possible doubts about the subject assigned approach; and h) the subject identiﬁes and represents variabilities in the e-commerce and Arcade Game Maker class models according to his/her given approach. Both, the e-commerce and AGM class models, were distributed in an equal number. The e-commerce was the ﬁrst, and the AGM, the second. The subjects were free to change the order of SPLs and their respective resolutions. The main task for each subject was reading and under- standing the e-commerce and Arcade Game Maker SPLs overviews. Then, the subjects annotated variabilities in the e-commerce and Arcade Game Maker class models.
spans.AnalysisProcedure: collected data was analyzed using appro- priate statistical methods, which are properly discussed in Section III-D. For each subject (“Subject #” col- umn), the following data for his/her given approach was collected: the number of correct and incorrect identiﬁed and represented variabilities; and the effectiveness cal- culation. These results are presented in Table IV. - analyze and interpret the X and Y collected data (sam- ple) by means of the Shapiro-Wilk normality test and the Mann-Whitney-Wilcoxon, to validate their statistical power; and - analyze and interpret the correlation between the effectiveness of the approaches and the subjects characterization questionnaire by means of Shapiro-Wilk normality tests and the Spearman’s ranking correlation techniques.
spans.Summary: Variability management is one of the most important activi- ties performed for the success of SPL adoption and evolution. Although several approaches for variability management are available, practically no effort has addressed empirical evalu- ation of such approaches. Industry needs empirical evidence of SPL variability management approaches for technology transfer. Existing literature does not provide such evidence, making the industry adoption process harder. In this paper, we are concerned on demonstrate the empirical evaluation of the SMarty effectiveness compared to the PLUS method for UML class models. Based on the obtained results, PLUS is more effective than SMarty for UML classes by taking into account two SPLs: e-commerce and AGM. As discussed (sections III-E and IV), such evidence might be related to the fact that PLUS has only two stereotypes to identify variability in class models (<< kernel >> and << optional >>). Although SMarty has more stereotypes and requires more discipline, it allows one to accurately iden- tify and represent variabilities in a non-ambiguous way, which is essential for generating consistent SPL speciﬁc products. In addition, SMarty is supported by a proper UML proﬁle, which is totally compliant with UML tools. Although we could not provide evidence of the SMarty effectiveness, this study contributed to the SMarty evolution based on both the results of the experiment carried out and the subjects? feedback. Therefore, new guidelines for class models were added to SMarty encompassing different class modeling elements, allowing a better training of the software engineers by the SMartyProcess and the improvement on the set of its guidelines.
spans.Impact: Besides the SMartyProcess, and its set of guidelines support the application of SMartyProﬁle, it is also a fundamental mechanism to facilitate the identiﬁcation and representation of variabilities. The agility, which is a consequence of the use of these guidelines, makes it feasible a faster adoption of SMarty than other approaches. Another beneﬁt of the use of the process is that it makes possible to identify new variabilities from an UML model, evolved the SPLs in general and also, the portfolio of products that can be instantiated.
spans.FutureWork: Thus, the experiment results cannot be generalize, which makes it clear that, as future work, new experiments must be planned and conducted taking into account the new version of SMarty (evolved) and real SPLs.

spans.Background: Feature models are considered a reference in the majority of Software Product Line (SPL) methods. There are several different feature model notations to represent requirements of an SPL, at a higher or lower level of abstraction. Some notations present properties to distinguish functional, conceptual and non-functional features of an SPL. Non-functional requirements, especially those that involve the construction of user interfaces (UI), are usually not represented in the feature models, since the user interfaces are often created manually for each product.
spans.Objective: In this paper we present an experimental study performed in order to evaluate the effort required to, as well as the beneﬁts and drawbacks of representing UI elements during the feature modeling of a Financial SPL.
spans.Methods: experimental study
spans.Results:
Our results indicate that the effort to use the notations are similar, but the use of the UI-
Odyssey-Fex notation provides a better representativeness of UI
elements.
spans.ProblemStatement:
Although there are many FM modeling notations available,
and a few of which supporting UI elements, SPL engineers
face some doubts when considering to model UI elements
into a FM, such as: Does an UI-supporting notation present
some advantage regarding ease of use when compared with a
standard FM notation?; What is the effort required to create
a FM with UI elements? Does the use of an UI-supporting
notation provide a better representativeness of UI elements?.
Despite these doubts, to the best of our knowledge there is
no work discussing the required modeling effort, beneﬁts and
issues on the use of notations that support the representation
of UI elements.
spans.ResearchObjectives:
in this paper we report an experimental study to provide evidence
about the advantage, the required effort to design the models
and representativeness of UI elements.
spans.Context:
A feature model (FM) represents all of the features, and the
relationships between them, of a software product line (SPL)
domain [1] [2] [5] [6]. A feature can be mandatory (must
be present in all of the derived products) or optional (one or
more domain products have this feature). A derived product is
composed by the mandatory features and a selection of optional
features.
spans.ExperimentalUnits:
As subjects, we invited undergraduate, master
and Ph.D. students from a university; from a company we
invited software engineers with some expertise in SPL. The
students were from Computer Science and Information Systems
courses. It is important to highlight that each student had a
different level of knowledge on SPL concepts, FM design and
UI element representation. For instance, some students had
some experience as a software analyst or as a developer, or
experience designing and developing software during an IT
course. The professional subjects were from an IT company,
with an advanced level of knowledge about SPL modeling, but
with an introductory knowledge on UI concepts. ... Total of Subjects
31
spans.ExperimentalMaterial:
The main experiment objects are
the FM diagrams designed by the subjects to model a ﬁnancial
SPL - one diagram for each notation. Moreover, other objects
were prepared and provided to support the subjects during the
execution of the experiments tasks, such as training material,
applications requirements, tools manual and examples of feature
model diagrams. To create the features models we have provided
a modeling supporting tool, called Odyssey [10].
spans.Tasks:
Session one - was used by the
subjects from the Group 1 to design the FM using the UI-
Odyssey-Fex notation, while subjects from Group 2 designed
the FM using the Odyssey-Fex notation. ... Session two - was used by
the Group 1 subjects to design the FM using the Odyssey-
Fex notation, while subjects from Group 2 designed the FM
using the UI-Odyssey-Fex notation. ... At the end of each session, all the subjects, from both groups,
answered the same survey, to evaluate the ease of use and
representativeness of each notation. For each survey question
we provided three close-ended options (Linkert scale): Disagree,
Neither agree nor disagree and Agree.
spans.Hypotheses:
RQ1: Null Hypothesis H0: There is no advantage, regarding ease of
use, when using Odyssey-Fex or UI-Odyssey-Fex notations. Al-
ternative Hypothesis H1: The use of UI-Odyssey-Fex notation
presents some advantage regarding ease of use when compared
with the Odyssey-Fex notation. Alternative Hypothesis H2:
The use of Odyssey-Fex notation presents some advantage
regarding ease of use when compared with the UI-Odyssey-Fex
notation.

RQ2: Null Hypothesis H0: The effort is the same when using
Odyssey-Fex or UI-Odyssey-Fex notations to design a feature
model. Alternative Hypothesis H1: The use of the UI-
Odyssey-Fex notation requires less effort to design a feature
model, when compared with the Odyssey-Fex notation. Alter-
native Hypothesis H2: The use of the Odyssey-Fex notation
requires less effort to design a feature model, when compared
with the UI-Odyssey-Fex notation.

RQ3: Null Hypothesis H0: The representativeness is the same,
when using the Odyssey-Fex or UI-Odyssey-Fex notations, to
represent UI elements. Alternative Hypothesis H1: The use
of the UI-Odyssey-Fex notation better represents UI elements
when compared with the Odyssey-Fex notation. Alternative
Hypothesis H2: The use of the Odyssey-Fex notation better
represents UI elements when compared with the UI-Odyssey-
Fex notation.
spans.IndependentVariables:
Independent variable = Odyssey-Fex and UI-
Odyssey-Fex notations
spans.DependentVariables:
Dependent variable = ease-of-use, effort required
and syntactic and semantic representativeness
spans.Procedure:
Our ﬁrst personal contact with the subjects was made through an
introductory presentation session, where an initial explanation
about the general idea of the experiment was presented. At this
ﬁrst moment we also provided a time slot, where the subjects
could ask open questions about the experiment setup as well
as about SPL and the FM notations and tools. At this moment
we also discussed the research goal and how the subjects’
data (e.g. experiment effort data) would be published. During
this ﬁrst session we presented the basics of software product
lines, FODA [5] and FeatuRSEB [15] methods, as well as the
Odyssey-Fex and UI-Odyssey-Fex notations. ... During the second session, performed in a different date,
manuals were presented to guide the use of the Odyssey-Fex
and UI-Odyssey-Fex notations and tools. At this time, all the
participants received instructions on the semantics of models,
as well as a detailed demonstration of how to use the tools.
At the ﬁnal part of the session it was presented an example
of a requirements document of a retail SPL (similar to a MD-
50 functional requirement document) and its correspondent
feature model. Based on this, it was possible to discuss and
answer questions from participants on the notations’ syntax,
such as on the use of tools. At the end of the session a subject
proﬁle form was provided to all the subjects. The information
extracted from the forms was used to classify and distribute
the subjects through the blocks before running the experiment.
To classify a subject into the blocks we used an ordinal scale
for each response of a multiple choice questionnaire [16]. For
instance, the subjects’ experience with SPL concepts and feature
modeling design was measured on a four level ordinal scale: 1 =
none, 2 = beginning level (studied in a class), 3 = intermediate
level (practised in a class project or in a small industry project),
4 = advanced level (used in more than one industrial project).
Based on this, we evaluated the average experience of each
subject and used it to distribute them into the blocks. The
distribution of the industrial and student subjects into the blocks
is depicted in Table I. ... The experiment execution phase was comprised of two sessions
(blue boxes in Figure 3): Session one - was used by the
subjects from the Group 1 to design the FM using the UI-
Odyssey-Fex notation, while subjects from Group 2 designed
the FM using the Odyssey-Fex notation. It is important to note
that to avoid misunderstanding, we provided the requirement
documents with only those requirements, seven requirements in
total, that the subject must design. Both groups used the same
application documents: requirements and models. Moreover,
they also designed the models at the same time, but they used
different and isolated lab rooms. Session two - was used by
the Group 1 subjects to design the FM using the Odyssey-
Fex notation, while subjects from Group 2 designed the FM
using the UI-Odyssey-Fex notation. As in the ﬁrst session, both
groups, separately, applied the same application documents that
had been provided previously in session one. It is important to
highlight the sessions one and two were performed in different
dates. To monitor the time spent by each subject, the researcher
who ran the experiment used a software to control the starting
and ending time of each subject. ... At the end of each session, all the subjects, from both groups,
answered the same survey, to evaluate the ease of use and
representativeness of each notation. For each survey question
we provided three close-ended options (Linkert scale): Disagree,
Neither agree nor disagree and Agree.
spans.Summary:
Requirements of a Software Product Line (SPL) are represented
with Feature Models. There are several notations for this
representation [6] [2] [15] [1] [3], which have distinct properties,
though all have the means to represent mandatory and optional
features of a system family within an SPL. Conversely, we have
observed that some notations do not cover the representation
of some non-functional aspects of an SPL, specially related to
User Interface (UI) elements.
To overcome this limitation, this research has analyzed the
representation of UI features in the building of Feature Models
(FM) in SPL, comparing the notation Odyssey-Fex with its
extension, UI-Odyssey-Fex. These notations were evaluated
based on three Research Questions (RQ), each of which meant
to evaluate advantages regarding ease-of-use, effort required
and syntactic and semantic representativeness, respectively.
The results show that regarding ease-of-use and required
effort, there is no statistically signiﬁcant difference between
the two notations. However, there is a signiﬁcant advantage
to representativeness in the use of UI-Odyssey-Fex, when
compared to Odyssey-Fex. We have identiﬁed two major threats to the experiment. The
ﬁrst is the size of the sample, as well as its being comprised
of a group that may not be representative of the population.
The second is the fact that the experiment only compares two
notations, whereas ideally a comparison with other common
notations, such as FODA, would be desirable.
spans.FutureWork:
In future works,
we hope to replicate this study with a different sample and
more notations, in order to provide a more strong evidences
about the beneﬁts and drawbacks of representing UI elements
using different FM notations.

  "Procedure": "Our ﬁrst personal contact with the subjects was made through an
introductory presentation session, where an initial explanation
about the general idea of the experiment was presented. At this
ﬁrst moment we also provided a time slot, where the subjects
could ask open questions about the experiment setup as well
as about SPL and the FM notations and tools. At this moment
we also discussed the research goal and how the subjects’
data (e.g. experiment effort data) would be published. During
this ﬁrst session we presented the basics of software product
lines, FODA [5] and FeatuRSEB [15] methods, as well as the
Odyssey-Fex and UI-Odyssey-Fex notations. ... During the second session, performed in a different date,
manuals were presented to guide the use of the Odyssey-Fex
and UI-Odyssey-Fex notations and tools. At this time, all the
participants received instructions on the semantics of models,
as well as a detailed demonstration of how to use the tools.
At the ﬁnal part of the session it was presented an example
of a requirements document of a retail SPL (similar to a MD-
50 functional requirement document) and its correspondent
feature model. Based on this, it was possible to discuss and
answer questions from participants on the notations’ syntax,
such as on the use of tools. At the end of the session a subject
proﬁle form was provided to all the subjects. The information
extracted from the forms was used to classify and distribute
the subjects through the blocks before running the experiment.
To classify a subject into the blocks we used an ordinal scale
for each response of a multiple choice questionnaire [16]. For
instance, the subjects’ experience with SPL concepts and feature
modeling design was measured on a four level ordinal scale: 1 =
none, 2 = beginning level (studied in a class), 3 = intermediate
level (practised in a class project or in a small industry project),
4 = advanced level (used in more than one industrial project).
Based on this, we evaluated the average experience of each
subject and used it to distribute them into the blocks. The
distribution of the industrial and student subjects into the blocks
is depicted in Table I. ... The experiment execution phase was comprised of two sessions
(blue boxes in Figure 3): Session one - was used by the
subjects from the Group 1 to design the FM using the UI-
Odyssey-Fex notation, while subjects from Group 2 designed
the FM using the Odyssey-Fex notation. It is important to note
that to avoid misunderstanding, we provided the requirement
documents with only those requirements, seven requirements in
total, that the subject must design. Both groups used the same
application documents: requirements and models. Moreover,
they also designed the models at the same time, but they used
different and isolated lab rooms. Session two - was used by
the Group 1 subjects to design the FM using the Odyssey-
Fex notation, while subjects from Group 2 designed the FM
using the UI-Odyssey-Fex notation. As in the ﬁrst session, both
groups, separately, applied the same application documents that
had been provided previously in session one. It is important to
highlight the sessions one and two were performed in different
dates. To monitor the time spent by each subject, the researcher
who ran the experiment used a software to control the starting
and ending time of each subject. ... At the end of each session, all the subjects, from both groups,
answered the same survey, to evaluate the ease of use and
representativeness of each notation. For each survey question
we provided three close-ended options (Linkert scale): Disagree,
Neither agree nor disagree and Agree.",
  "Summary": "Requirements of a Software Product Line (SPL) are represented
with Feature Models. There are several notations for this
representation [6] [2] [15] [1] [3], which have distinct properties,
though all have the means to represent mandatory and optional
features of a system family within an SPL. Conversely, we have
observed that some notations do not cover the representation
of some non-functional aspects of an SPL, specially related to
User Interface (UI) elements.
To overcome this limitation, this research has analyzed the
representation of UI features in the building of Feature Models
(FM) in SPL, comparing the notation Odyssey-Fex with its
extension, UI-Odyssey-Fex. These notations were evaluated
based on three Research Questions (RQ), each of which meant
to evaluate advantages regarding ease-of-use, effort required
and syntactic and semantic representativeness, respectively.
The results show that regarding ease-of-use and required
effort, there is no statistically signiﬁcant difference between
the two notations. However, there is a signiﬁcant advantage
to representativeness in the use of UI-Odyssey-Fex, when
compared to Odyssey-Fex. We have identiﬁed two major threats to the experiment. The
ﬁrst is the size of the sample, as well as its being comprised
of a group that may not be representative of the population.
The second is the fact that the experiment only compares two
notations, whereas ideally a comparison with other common
notations, such as FODA, would be desirable.",
  "FutureWork": "In future works,
we hope to replicate this study with a different sample and
more notations, in order to provide a more strong evidences
about the beneﬁts and drawbacks of representing UI elements
using different FM notations."
}

spans.Background: Feature modeling is a popular Software Product Line Engi- neering (SPLE) technique used to describe variability in a product family. A usable feature modeling tool environment should enable SPLE prac- titioners to produce good quality models, in particular, models that ef- fectively communicate modeled information. FAMILIAR is a text-based environment for manipulating and composing Feature Models (FMs).
spans.Objective: In this paper we present extensions we made to FAMILIAR to enhance its usability. The extensions include a visualization of FMs, or more pre- cisely, a feature diagram rendering mechanism that supports the use of a combination of text and graphics to describe FMs, their conﬁgurations, and the results of FM analyses.
spans.Methods: preliminary experiment
spans.Results: The preliminary experiment provides some evidence that use of the new environment results in increased cognitive eﬀectiveness of novice users and improved quality of new FMs.
spans.ProblemStatement: A number of textual domain-speciﬁc modeling languages (DSMLs) for feature modeling [6][7][11][15][21], including FAMILIAR [2–4, 16], have been proposed during the last decade. There are many beneﬁts to using text-based languages to describe the variability [12]. For example, a lightweight textual language can leverage already established tools that are available for editing and manipulat- ing textual language statements. Such support facilitates rapid prototyping of a DSML. Other desirable characteristics that typically come with expressive tex- tual notations with good tool support include interoperability with other textual DSMLs, and scripting support that enables replay of operation sequences, and modular management of scripts [4]. On the other hand, creating and analyzing a large text-based feature model (FM) often requires signiﬁcant cognitive eﬀort.
spans.ResearchObjectives: Our work on extending a textual DSML for FMs and on evalu- ating the resulting FM development environment is motivated by the following question: Does the lack of support for visualizing FMs in FM development tools hinder the usability of these tools when managing multiple and large FMs during modeling sessions?
spans.Context: Feature models (FM) are often used in Software Product Line Engineering (SPLE) to describe variability in a product family. A usable feature model- ing tool environment should enable SPLE practitioners to produce good quality models, in particular, models that eﬀectively communicate modeled information.
spans.Goals: Evaluate the FAMILIAR Tool to better understand the impact on usabil- ity aspects of implementing feature model visualizations on the FAMILIAR language from the viewpoint of modelers.
spans.ExperimentalUnits: The controlled experiment was conducted within two groups of gradu- ate Computer Science students with a total of 16 participants from two countries, United States and France. The ﬁrst group involved 3 graduate Ph.D. students that are under Dr. Robert France’s supervision at the Colorado State University (CSU). The second group involved 13 Masters and Ph.D. students that took a graduate SPL course taught by Dr. Philippe Collet, at the University of Nice, Sophia Antipolis (UNS).
spans.Tasks: (1) Basic training on SPL, Feature Modeling, and the FAMILIAR language, (2) conﬁguring the FA- MILIAR environment in preparation for the experiment, and (3) the experiment session. ... (3.1) analyzing the on-line conﬁgurator for Audi cars, and then (3.2) modeling it by creating a new FM ﬁle for the Audi conﬁgurator.
spans.Hypotheses: Using the FAMILIAR Tool with visualized feature models yields higher FM quality, user eﬀectiveness, and eﬃciency than using the same tool with text only mode, when creating new FMs.
spans.IndependentVariables: choice of the used tool is the independent variable
spans.DependentVariables: FM quality, user eﬀectiveness, and user eﬃciency are the dependent variables.
spans.Procedure: These stages involved the following: (1) Basic training on SPL, Feature Modeling, and the FAMILIAR language, (2) conﬁguring the FA- MILIAR environment in preparation for the experiment, and (3) the experiment session. The UNS participants, a larger sample, formed the treatment group by working only with the new FAMILIAR Tool (Visual). On the other hand, CSU participants formed the control group by working only with the legacy standalone tool (Text-based). ... the experiment session was no longer than 55 minutes, and it consisted of two sub-tasks (3.1) analyzing the on-line conﬁgurator for Audi cars, and then (3.2) modeling it by creating a new FM ﬁle for the Audi conﬁgurator. Students were asked to work at their own pace, independently of one another. They were also required to record all of their interactions with the tools during the experiment session. By doing this, we could accurately measure the number of modeling tasks that users successfully completed, the accuracy with which users com- pleted tasks (i.e., some quantiﬁcation of the errors), the duration of tasks, users’ learning of the interface, and ﬁnally, asses quality of FMs created, and calculate user eﬃciency and eﬀectiveness.
spans.AnalysisProcedure: Dependent Variable - FM Quality: According to the MUSiC method, qual- ity is a measure of the degree to which the output achieves the task goals. For the purpose of this experiment, quality is expressed in terms of a ﬁnal FM quality. Table 2 breaks down the criteria that we used to assess the quality of an FM. ... Dependent Variable - User Eﬀectiveness: To assess user eﬀectiveness, we deﬁned a quantity that is a measure of the amount of a task completed by a user. ... Table 3 shows how we calculated quantity as a measure of FM completeness. Finally, the user eﬀectiveness is given as a percentage, and is calculated using the following formula: UserEffectiveness = (FMQuantity ∗FMQuality)% ... Dependent Variable - User Eﬃciency: Note that the user eﬀectiveness does not take into account the time required to complete a given task. The user eﬃciency calculation does include the time component. The user eﬃciency is calculated using the following formula: UserEfficiency = UserEffectiveness / ScenarioT ime
spans.Summary: In this paper we presented an extension of a textual DSML for feature modeling and an evaluation of the resulting development environment. The evaluation aimed at answering the question: Does the lack of support for visualizing FMs in FM development tools hinder the usability of these tools when managing multiple and large FMs during modeling sessions? We found evidence that using the new FAMILIAR Tool with visualized FMs resulted in an increased cognitive eﬃciency and eﬀectiveness of novice practi- tioners which also led to the improved quality of FMs they created. To the best of our knowledge, this is the ﬁrst work which describes and evaluates com- bined graphical-textual tooling for feature modeling. Having essentially the same underlying environment for both FAMILIAR tools allowed us to observe the po- tential beneﬁts of FM visualization, without interfering diﬀerences that would likely arise from using diﬀerent tools. However, an experiment on a larger scale would be required to identify whether this outcome would hold for SPL experts that work with larger and scripted FMs.
spans.FutureWork: A larger scale experiment is thus in our immediate future work plan. The FAMILIAR language has capabilities to manipulate several FMs, to write scripts that inputs and outputs FMs and other relevant types such as conﬁgurations. We also want to investigate appropriate visual support when dealing with these operations. To do so, we plan to provide feature diagram visualizations with a more compact form using aggregated values and indicators. In the longer term, we want to tackle issues related to the evolution of feature models, as well as relationships between several FMs, as in multiple software product lines. We expect these advances to provide support and insights for a better and wider usage of feature modeling in software product line engineering.

spans.Background:
Explicit variability management is essential for large product 
lines and requires explicit strategies for instantiating the 
managed variabilities during application engineering. An 
instantiation strategy proposes a certain order for the resolution 
of variabilities during application engineering or for testing. If 
an alphabetical strategy is used, for instance, the variabilities 
are resolved in alphabetical order, from A to Z.
spans.Objective:
In this paper, 
we motivate the necessity of strategies for large variability 
models, which help to identify starting points and guide the 
resolution of variability models.
spans.Methods:
We sketch the application of the strategies in a tool and give 
the results of an experiment performed to compare the 
strategies in different situations.
spans.Results:
The experiment showed that 
the efficiency of instantiation differs by more than 35% 
between different strategies. Additionally, the meaningfulness 
of the instantiation was perceived differently for the various 
strategies and the strategies were all perceived as being easy to 
resolve.
spans.Conclusions:
With the experiment, we managed to demonstrate that 
the effectiveness of instantiation strategies differs, which 
motivates the need for different variability instantiation 
strategies in different situations.
spans.ProblemStatement:
Even though software 
product line engineering solves several issues, it also imposes 
new challenges. One challenge is the management of software 
variability. The term commonalities is often used to refer to 
reusable artifacts or artifact parts that are being reused as-is 
among different products, while the term variabilities is used to 
refer to reusable artifacts or artifact parts that vary and hence 
need tailoring when used in a product. To design this tailoring 
process as effectively as possible, the variabilities have to be 
managed explicitly and in an orthogonal way [11][19]. Thus, 
variability management comprises all activities needed to 
explicitly model, manage, and document those parts, which 
vary among the products of a product line. Managing and 
instantiating variations at different levels of abstraction and 
across all generic development artifacts is a daunting task, 
especially when the systems supporting various products are 
very large, as is common in an industrial setting [2][3]. With 
large systems, the necessity of instantiating variabilities in a 
structured and systematic way is obvious, as variability models 
are large and complex.
spans.ResearchObjectives:
In this paper, we motivate the necessity 
of strategies for large variability models, which help to identify 
starting points and guide the resolution of variability models.
spans.Context:
Software product line engineering is an approach that develops 
and maintains families of products while taking advantage of 
their common aspects and predicted variabilities [4][11]. 
Software product line engineering is currently one of the most 
promising methodologies at hand to achieve high-quality 
requirements, to supply different customers with a certain 
software product tailored to their needs, and to reduce 
development and maintenance costs.
spans.Goals:
The goal of the experiment was to compare the efficiency and 
meaningfulness of the strategies in settings that are as realistic 
as possible.
spans.ExperimentalUnits:
The subjects of this experiment were 14 
students, most of them from the Master of Software 
Engineering program, who attended the Product Line lectures. 
The majority (50%) had no previous experience with product 
lines. The participants did not have strong experience with 
software development: 50% of them reported 1-3 years of 
experience, while 29% had no experience at all. 79% majored 
in computer science or computer science related courses.
spans.ExperimentalMaterial:
In order to be at least partially independent of any specific 
model, we implemented three different decision models from 
different domains from the CVT project or form earlier 
projects. Table 2 shows the characteristics of those models. 
The models were of comparable size. One model had a higher 
constraint density (# constraints/ #decisions in the decision 
model) 
one 
model 
had 
a 
higher 
folder 
density 
(#folders(components)/ #decisions in the decision model). The 
tree hierarchy was always one. ... The characteristics described in the table can affect the 
strategies in different ways: 
x Number of constraints, constraint density: influence most 
constraining and most constrained orders; the more 
constraints, the faster the resolution with these strategies.  
x Number of folders, folder density: influence DFS and BFS.  
x A high number for hierarchy depth might benefit the DFS 
order and harm the BFS order. If the model is more or less 
level, both strategies should lead to the same results. 
x Naming convention: Influences the alphabetical order, e.g., 
if all decisions related to a specific component have the 
same prefix, then the alphabetical order can be semantically 
meaningful since there is no need to change the context all 
the time.
spans.Hypotheses:
H1: Effectiveness in variability instantiation differs 
significantly based on the strategy. 
H2: Choosing the right strategy for the right situation can 
lower the effort for variability instantiation to a large extent.
spans.IndependentVariables:
x The strategy to be applied: We wanted to analyze 
different strategies in different situations. 
x The model to be instantiated: We wanted to be independent 
of a concrete model.
spans.DependentVariables:
Effectiveness = 
Median 
(Efficiency 
+ 
Easiness 
+ 
Meaningfulness)
spans.Procedure:
The experiment was executed in two runs. The first execution 
had nine participants and the second one six. One person 
participated twice. ... The first 30 minutes of the first run were used for explanations: 
underlying concepts, tool demonstration, and explanation 
about the task. The actual run took 1h. 
The second run was executed within 30 minutes as the students 
had to leave early. Again, the first 30 minutes were used for 
explanation and 30 minutes were used for executing the tasks. 
During the explanation phase, three combinations of model and 
strategy were used by the participants as test cases in order to 
become familiar with the tool. In the first run, the nine 
participants were randomly divided into three different groups. 
Each received two models and should instantiate them in 
different orders according to the six implemented strategies in 
order to minimize the learning effect of working with the tool 
and the models. Each strategy resolution should be executed in 
a different situation: 
x
Random selection: always choose the topmost value to 
answer the questions 
x
Personal selection: choose the value that you think fits the 
question best 
x
Pre-defined values: use the value in the table to answer the 
questions 
We used the situations as placeholders for real instantiation 
situations: Random selection will often be done for testing the 
variability management tool or the variability model during 
family engineering, personal selection will be done by the 
customer during application engineering, and pre-defined 
selection will be done by an application engineer.  
The total number of executions expected from each participant 
was 36 (6 different strategies per model, 3 different situations). 
However, some of them were unable to finish all instantiations 
within one hour.  
In the second run, the students were also divided into three 
groups, but because of the shorter time for the experiment run, 
we simplified the task: Each student was to instantiate a model 
using four different strategies, this time using the pre-defined 
set of values. Two sets of values for each model were 
provided. In both runs, we gave the students a questionnaire in 
which they should provide their background. Additionally, 
they had to rate each model on a 4-point Likert scale [23] of 
“strongly disagree, disagree, agree, strongly agree” according 
to the two questions: "It was easy to instantiate this model" and 
"The model was instantiated in a reasonable/sensible order". 
By answering these questions, they thus rated the easiness of 
the instantiation and the meaningfulness of the model 
instantiated with a certain strategy.
spans.AnalysisProcedure:
For each execution of the resolution wizard, the following data 
was collected automatically in a log file: group name/id, 
selected strategy execution time,  duration, number of clicks, 
status: finished execution or canceled. 
The log files were then processed using a Java program 
especially designed for that purpose (we will provide a website 
with the Java program and the raw data soon) and the resulting

spans.Summary:
In this paper, we described the evaluation of a collection of 
instantiation strategies for variability management for product 
lines. These strategies can be used for orthogonal variability 
management during product line engineering to identify an 
optimal 
order 
of 
decision 
resolutions 
in 
application 
engineering. We have identified ten strategies so far (plus 
combinations of them) and implemented six of them in the 
tool. The remaining four will be implemented in the near 
future. We performed an experiment with students where we 
managed to show that the efficiency of instantiation differs by 
37% when choosing different resolution strategies and the 
meaningfulness of the instantiations was perceived differently 
with different strategies and different instantiation situations 
(like random instantiation for testing or fixed instantiation for 
product derivation). Overall, we were able to show that the 
effectiveness of the instantiation (as a combination of 
efficiency, easiness, and meaningfulness) differed and that the 
instantiation by folder/component was seen as the most 
effective strategy.
spans.FutureWork:
As further work on the experiment, we 
would like to see if there is a difference between the theoretical 
resolution time (computable by <number of resolution steps 
with a given strategy> * <average time for one resolution>) 
and, if there is one, analyze this difference further. In [12], we 
already analyzed different contexts (e.g., large/small model, 
amount of knowledge available, development process, etc.) 
and the different instantiation situations for variability 
instantiation in product lines mentioned above. We plan to 
analyze these context factors more thoroughly, perform further 
case studies, and combine them with the experiment results in 
order to ultimately get a framework that can suggest good 
instantiation strategies for a given product line instantiation 
situation. For this framework, we would need more and larger 
case studies to compare and characterize real-life situations 
and select good (or bad) strategies depending on the 
characteristics of the model and of the product line.

spans.Background: Dynamic Software Product Lines (DSPL) is a promising approach to enable variability management at run-time. As a particularly novel approach, variability management at runtime demands proper guidance for software engineers. Although there is a number of variability modeling techniques, understand whether they fulﬁll important requirements to deal with the DSPL challenges is necessary.
spans.Objective: In this work, we ana-lyzed two variability modeling techniques with regard to their effectiveness and efﬁciency
spans.Methods: controlled experiment
spans.Results: The results showed Context-aware Feature Model technique more effective than Tropos Goal Model with Context technique considering precision. Nevertheless, both techniques were effective considering recall.
spans.ProblemStatement: Although variability modeling is widely described in the SPL literature, it still lacks an adequate support for software engineers to decide the most suitable variability modeling technique for DSPL. The literature has addressed some approaches to deal with dynamic variability in DSPLs [4] [5] by adapting or extending variability modeling techniques from SPL. However, choosing the most suitable technique and understanding whether it has enough requirements to meet the needs of a given DSPL application domain is far from trivial.
spans.ResearchObjectives: In our previous work [11], we investigated the literature by identifying the main variability modeling techniques for DSPL and deﬁned a set of evaluation criteria to rank these ap-proaches. This rank aimed to analyze and categorize variability modeling techniques. In such an investigation, we noticed a lack of empirical studies addressing the assessment of existing techniques, particularly in the sense of techniques selection to use in complex application domains.
spans.Context: The adaptation of the product line to generate speciﬁc prod-ucts in SPL engineering is commonly handled at development time. However, emerging domains have demanded adaptations to occur during system execution, i.e., at runtime. Mobile devices [4] and smart homes [5] are examples of domains that commonly demand runtime adaptations, so they can deal with either users’ needs or environment constraints seamlessly [6]. Dynamic Software Product Lines (DSPL) elaborates on the SPL engineering principles by improving the capability of handling with software-variant binding at runtime [7].
spans.Goals: This experimental study is aimed to analyze Variability Modeling Techniques for Dynamic Software Product Lines for the purpose of evaluating them with regard to its effective-ness and efﬁciency from the viewpoint of SPL researchers in the context of undergraduate, M.Sc. and Ph.D. students modeling a Smart Home DSPL project.
spans.ExperimentalUnits: The experiment was con-ducted in an academic environment with students from Federal University of Bahia, as follows: one undergraduate student, three M.Sc. students and six Ph.D. students.
spans.ExperimentalMaterial: We used two types of forms: the background form to characterize the subjects according to their experience and expertise; and the feedback form to gather information about the techniques and the experiment execution. In the training session, we used the presentation content with concepts related to the experiment. In this session, we also performed training exercises, thus, materials including a small project and instructions for their execution were given to the subjects. In the experiment execution, we provided a guideline with instructions on how to model using both techniques and the experimental task description. The task content included the smart home project, comprising its functional and contextual requirements.
spans.Tasks: In this step, the subjects received a software modeling problem, based on a DSPL project in the smart homes domain. This problem was described by means of instructions for the proper system functioning. In fact, these instructions repre-sented functional and contextual requirements, the subjects should read and interpret them. In the functional requirements, the subjects could gather functions, variability and constraints of the software system. In the contextual requirements, the subjects could gather context information and their relationship to the system functions. Each subject performed the activity by modeling the prob-lem using both techniques A and B. They had free time to perform it and received instructions to take notes of the start and end time for each task performed. We did not use support tools to aid this activity. The subjects received only a sheet and a pencil to perform the tasks. This activity followed the same set of the training exercise, thus, the subjects could concentrate only in the solution to the activity problem.

Effectiveness Hypotheses

H10: EPT A = EPT B
H30: EPTT A = EPTT B
H1a: EPT A <> EPT B
H1a1: EPT A > EPT B

H3a1: EPTT A > EPTT B
