De- pending on the concrete application domain and the respective level of mission- /safety-criticality, it is imperative, or even enforced by industrial standards, to guarantee a certain degree of code coverage for every delivered product [11]. The computational problem underlying automated test generation consists of expen- sive reachability analyses of the program state space. Symbolic model checking has emerged in the past as a promising approach for fully automated white- box test generation using counterexamples as test inputs [7]. However, in case of large sets of complex test goals, scalability issues still hinder eﬃcient test- case generation when being performed for every test goal anew. This is even worse when generating test inputs for covering entire product-line implemen- tations. To avoid product-by-product (re-)generation of test cases with many redundant generation runs, a family-based test-generation approach must en- hance test-suite-derivation techniques to be likewise applicable to product-line implementations [12,24].",
  "ResearchObjectives": "In this paper, we present a novel approach for eﬃcient white-box test-suite generation that guarantees multi-goal test coverage of product-line implementa- tions. The approach systematically exploits reuse potential among reachability- analysis results by means of similarity among test cases – derived for diﬀerent test goals [8], and/or – derived for diﬀerent product variants [12].",
  "Context": "Software-product-line engineering [15] has become a key technology to cope with the variability of highly-conﬁgurable (software) systems, prevalent in various ap- plication domains today. In recent years, software product lines (SPL) have found their way into numerous industrial application domains, e.g., automotive, information and mobile systems [29]. SPL engineering aims at developing a family of similar, yet well-distinguished software products based on a common core plat- form, where commonality and variability among the family members (product variants) are explicitly speciﬁed in terms of features. Each feature corresponds to (1) user-visible product characteristics in the problem domain, relevant for product conﬁguration, as well as to (2) composable implementation artifacts for (automated) assembling of implementation variants. This philosophy of ex- tensive reuse of common feature artifacts among product variants facilitates a remarkable gain in eﬃciency compared to one-by-one variant development [15].",
  "Goals": "To investigate the eﬀects of the two proposed reuse strategies, we compare both of them to a product-by-product (PbP) product-line test-suite generation ap- proach.",
  "ExperimentalUnits": "For our experiments, we se- lected two subject systems that are well-known from several benchmarks, e.g., in context of product-line veriﬁcation and feature interaction detection [3]. – Mine-Pump (MP) implements a water pump system based on the CONIC project [20]. The product-line implementation has 279 LoC, 7 features, e.g., a methane sensor, and 64 conﬁgurations. – E-Mail (EM) is based on a model of an e-mail system developed by Hall [18]. The product-line implementation we used has 233 LoC, 4 features, e.g., en- cryption and automatic forwarding, and 8 conﬁgurations.",
  "ExperimentalMaterial": "To answer the research questions, we implemented a product-line test-suite gen- erator based on CPA/tiger1, a test-case generator on top of CPAchecker2, which is a software model checker for C programs. Internally, CPAchecker uses CFA and ARG representations and applies the CEGAR approach, as described in Sect. 3. Furthermore, we use FQL3 (FShell Query Language), which is part of CPA/tiger, to specify complex coverage criteria. For a variability-aware gener- ation of product-line test suites, we integrated a BDD-based feature-parameter analysis into CPA/tiger and added further code to determine which test goals of which variants are covered by a given test case.",
  "IndependentVariables": "For quantifying the eﬀects of reuse among product variants, we apply a family-based (FB), i.e., variability-aware, generation approach, whereas for the reuse among test goals (TG), we apply a PbP approach. Finally, we combine both reuse strategies (FBTG) to measure potential synergies.",
  "DependentVariables": "Our measurements, e.g., the CPU time and the number of model-checker calls, were obtained by hooking into the test-case generator.",
  "Procedure": "As coverage criterion, we applied Basic-Block Coverage, i.e., each basic state- ment block constitutes a test goal. Our measurements, e.g., the CPU time and the number of model-checker calls, were obtained by hooking into the test-case generator. We performed our evaluation on a E5-2650 (2 GHz) machine with 30 GB of RAM. CPA/tiger ran with value-based analysis, an overall timeout of 24 h, and a timeout per test goal of 900 s, i.e., if a test goal had not been reached after 900 s, the next test goal was processed.",

spans.Background: A software product line (SPL) is a family of programs that are differ- entiated by features — increments in functionality. Systematically testing an SPL is challenging because it requires running each test of a test suite against a combinatorial number of programs. Feature models capture dependencies among features and can (1) reduce the space of programs to test and (2) enable accurate categorization of failing tests as failures of programs or the tests themselves, not as failures due to illegal combinations of features. In practice, sadly, feature models are not always available.
spans.Objective: We introduce SPLif, the ﬁrst approach for testing SPLs that does not require the a priori availability of feature models. Our insight is to use a proﬁle of passing and failing test runs to quickly identify failures that are indicative of real problems in test or code rather than specious failures due to illegal feature combinations.
spans.Results: Experimental results on ﬁve SPLs and one large conﬁgurable system (GCC) demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach. SPLif enabled the discovery of ﬁve news bugs in GCC, three of which have already been ﬁxed.
spans.ProblemStatement: We address the important problem of ﬁnding tests that fail on legal conﬁgurations of SPLs regardless of how complete a feature model may be. Intuitively, only tests that fail on legal conﬁgurations indicate real faults so ﬁnding such fault-revealing legal conﬁgura- tions soon is important for quick bug detection.
spans.ResearchObjectives: It is important to note that this problem is distinct compared to reverse-engineering feature models from code [5,7,8,18,21,32,42, 50,56]. Although it is possible to use testing to complement existing feature models the goal of this paper is to detect legal fault-revealing conﬁgurations quickly.
spans.Context: Software product lines (SPLs) improve the quality and reduce maintenance costs for a family of related programs [45,52]. Each program of an SPL is identiﬁed by a unique combination of features – increments in functionality. SPLs can be constructed using feature variables, which guard the execution of feature-speciﬁc code (in the spirit of ifdef preprocessing directives) [11,17].
spans.Goals: We pose the following research questions to evaluate SPLif: RQ1 How well does SPLif rank faulty tests for inspection? RQ2 How well does SPLif rank conﬁgurations (of selected tests) for inspection?
spans.ExperimentalUnits: We initially evaluated SPLif using ﬁve small subjects (size range: 1.7–3.6KLOC) that were used to test SPLs previously. Figure 4 tabulates, for each subject, the source of the subject, the number of feature variables, the number of valid (complete) conﬁg- urations, and the code size. ... Subjects: Companies, DesktopSearcher, GPL, Notepad, and ZipMe
spans.ExperimentalMaterial: FEST framework ... SPLat tool
spans.Procedure: We asked 5 students to create tests. We assigned two subjects per student and two students per subject, and provided instructions on how to create tests. In brief, we instructed students to create a test suite that achieves maximum feature coverage. Detailed instructions that students received for creating tests can be found elsewhere [24]. We provided support to students on how to use the FEST framework [25] to create GUI tests for DesktopSearcher and Notepad.
spans.Summary: Software Product Lines (SPLs) are an important design and imple- mentation paradigm for controlling variability in families of related software products. Testing SPLs is important as the volume of re- search on that topic indicates. Prior research makes the assumption that SPLs come equipped with complete, formally speciﬁed feature models. Unfortunately, this assumption does not always hold. We presented SPLif, a new approach for testing SPLs with incom- plete feature models, or even no feature model at all. SPLif helps the user prioritize failing tests and conﬁgurations for inspection. Our experiments showed that SPLif is promising and can scale to large systems, such as GCC.
spans.FutureWork: In the near future, we plan to apply SPLif to other large conﬁgurable systems and to optimize execution by leveraging the similarities across multiple similar states [20,36,44].

spans.Background: Testing every member of a product line individually is of- ten impracticable due to large number of possible product conﬁgurations. Thus, feature models are frequently used to generate samples, i.e., subsets of product conﬁgurations under test. Besides the extensively studied combinatorial interaction testing (CIT) approach for coverage-driven sam- ple generation, only few approaches exist so far adopting mutation testing to emulate faults in feature models to be detected by a sample.
spans.Objective: In this paper, we present a mutation- based sampling framework for fault-based product-line test- ing.
spans.Methods: We deﬁne a comprehensive catalog of atomic mutation operators on the graphical representation of feature models. This way, we are able (1) to also deﬁne complex mutation operators emulating more subtle faults, and (2) to classify operators semantically, e.g., to avoid redundant and equiv- alent mutants. We further introduce similarity-based mu- tant selection and higher order mutation strategies to reduce testing eﬀorts. Our implementation is based on the graph transformation engine Henshin and is evaluated concerning eﬀectiveness/eﬃciency trade-oﬀs.
spans.ProblemStatement: Most of these approaches consider the feature model of the respective product-line under test as input, and automati- cally generate preferably small samples, meeting the cor- responding combinatorial coverage criterion. Feature mod- els provide an intuitive graphical layout by means of a fea- ture diagram, organizing the set of features in a tree-like hierarchical structure, equipped with further modeling el- ements to denote diﬀerent kinds of constraints. However, although pairwise CIT has particularly turned out to consti- tute a well-suited heuristic for eﬃcient SPL testing, one ma- jor drawback of CIT is its purely black-box nature, i.e., usu- ally not incorporating any further domain knowledge such as the fault history of (combinations of) features, which may obstruct eﬀectiveness. As a result, a sample may contain many redundant/unimportant feature combinations, as well as potentially missing important/error-prone ones beyond T-wise [10, 26]. To overcome these deﬁciencies, the adoption of fault-based test selection strategies also to product-line sampling has been recently proposed by Henard et al. [11]. In particular, mutation operators are applied to feature mod- els in order to emulate potential faults by means of small changes in product-line speciﬁcations. This approach can be applied in two ways, namely (1) to measure the quality of ex- isting sampling approaches with respect to their mutant de- tection ratio, and (2) to generate mutant-covering samples. Although this approach has shown promising improvements compared to CIT, it is yet limited in several ways. First, mutation operators are deﬁned as basic changes at the level of propositional formulae representations of feature models rather than the graphical representation. As a consequence, meaningful semantic information only present at the graphi- cal level of the feature diagram may get lost, thus potentially failing to capture subtle faults in terms of mutations aﬀect- ing complex feature diagram fragments. Second, it lacks an a-priori classiﬁcation of the semantic impacts of mutations, e.g., in order to avoid equivalent mutants [15]. Finally, no systematic strategies for reducing the number of mutants have been investigated so far, thus potentially leading to a quickly growing number of mutants, especially in case of large-scale feature models.
spans.ResearchObjectives: In this paper, we present a comprehensive framework for fault-based assessment, improvement and (re-)generation of conﬁguration samples for eﬀective and scalable product-line testing based on feature-diagram mutation.
spans.Context: Software product lines (SPL) provide a viable means to cope with the ever-growing diversity of modern software sys- tems [8]. In an SPL, the diﬀerent members of a family of sim- ilar software products are explicitly distinguished by means of their features. Each feature, therefore, constitutes a user- visible product characteristic explicitly conﬁgurable by the customer. As a result, the number of possible product con- ﬁgurations grows exponentially in the number of available features, where feature models are frequently used to im- pose further constraints on the validity of feature combina- tions. This well-known problem of exponential explosion of the number of possible product conﬁgurations in combina- tion with complex conﬁgurations constraints makes analysis of entire product lines a very challenging task [30]. For in- stance, testing every individual product of a product line is, in general, impracticable for real-world applications, often comprising up to thousands of features [32], due to limited amount of time and resources [25].
spans.Goals: For the evaluation of the presented mutation-based sam- pling approach for eﬀective SPL testing, we consider the following research questions. RQ1 (Applicability). Is the developed feature-diagram mu- tation procedure applicable to arbitrary input data sets? RQ2 (Eﬀectiveness). Does the developed mutation-based sample improvement strategy increase testing eﬀec- tiveness of CIT samples without drastically obstruct- ing testing eﬃciency? RQ3 (Eﬃciency). Does a purely mutation-based sample- selection strategy improve testing eﬃciency compared to CIT sampling and how do mutation reduction strate- gies decrease eﬀectiveness?
spans.ExperimentalUnits: Feature-diagram mutation framework
spans.ExperimentalMaterial: To address RQ1–RQ3, we conducted experiments on a cor- pus consisting of two kinds of input data sets: (A) The bench-scale PPU SPL case study already discussed throughout this paper. For this real-world case study consisting of 19 features, we have full access to imple- mentation details and the development history, which allows us to design mutation scenarios that emulate realistic faults; (B) We applied the BeTTy generator [29] to generate artiﬁcial input data sets comprising feature diagrams of sizes between 50–500 (step-width of 50) nodes, which is usually considered industrial strength. As further complexity values, e.g., concerning the relative number of alternative-groups, we applied characteristic data gained from experiences from real-world case studies such as the PPU SPL, as well as from interviews with domain experts. ... We run all experiments on an AMD Phenom X4 quad core processor, with 3.6GHZ and 16GB Ram with Windows 8.1 and Java 8.
spans.IndependentVariables: Independent variable = sample selection (approach with CIT sampling and pure black-box CIT)
spans.DependentVariables: Dependent variable = SPL testing efficiency and effectiveness.
spans.Procedure: For classical sample generation, we used CIT sampling of strength T from 1 to 3 and 100% coverage each. We neglected experiments with samples for T=3 and num- ber of features > 200 as the generation time exceeded 24 hours. For addressing RQ1–RQ3, we applied all 9 de- tectable atomic mutation operators (see Table 1), as well as the complex operator depicted in Fig. 3. As mutation reduction strategy, we used Similarity-based Selection with radius of 1 to take direct neighbors into consideration for ranking. As coverage criterion, we applied 50% coverage, a minimum number of 1 and a maximum number of 50 selected candidates. To compensate deviation, e.g., with respect to CPU time, all experiments were conducted 3 times each, where the average value has been taken as result.
spans.Summary: We presented a comprehensive feature-diagram mutation framework for generating eﬀective and eﬃcient samples for fault-based SPL testing. The framework consists of a catalog of atomic, as well as complex mutation operators, together with a semantic classiﬁcation of their semantic change im- pact. We further propose parametrized mutation applica- tion strategies to control the number of generated mutants, i.e., mutation selection and higher-order mutation. The ap- proach is fully implemented in a tool based on the graph transformation engine Henshin. Our evaluation results ob- tained from various experiments show that a combination of our approach with pairwise CIT sampling leads to improve- ments concerning both SPL testing eﬃciency and eﬀective- ness compared to pure black-box CIT sample selection.
spans.FutureWork: As a future work, we plan to conduct further experiments, e.g., to compare our results with similar approaches [11, 3]. We also plan to further study higher-order mutation and complex mutation operations, e.g., simulating frequent faults in diﬀerent application domains. Finally, we plan to combine feature-diagram mutations with mutations on fea- ture implementation artifacts.

spans.Background:
Testing variability intensive systems is a formidable 
task due to the combinatorial explosion of feature interactions 
that result from all variations.
spans.Objective:
We developed and validated an 
approach of combinatorial test generation using Multi-
Perspective Feature Models (MPFM). MPFMs are a set of 
feature models created to achieve Separation of Concerns within 
the model.
spans.Results:
This approach improves test coverage of variability. 
Results from an experiment on a real-life case show that up to 
37% of the test effort could be reduced and up to 79% defects 
from the live system could be detected. We discuss the learning 
from this experiment and further research potential in testing 
variability intensive systems.
spans.ProblemStatement:
One of the characteristics of a VIS is the combinatorial 
explosion of variability. Feature interactions occur when 
inclusion of a feature in the system modifies the behavior of 
other features. VIS are likely to have a large number of such 
interactions due to their inherent characteristics viz. 
Configurability, Customizability. This means that, when a 
feature is added or modified, one has to ensure that it works in 
conjunction with all the variations that each configuration may 
have. This can be a formidable task for a real-world system, 
where the number of variations is large. 
The distributed nature of teams in software services 
industry pose additional challenges, such as: lack of access to 
software artifacts, difficulty in analyzing change impact, 
insufficient domain understanding and so on. Inability to 
identify change impact accurately, makes it imperative that all 
variations be tested. Resource constraints pose another 
challenge – it may not be possible to run all the tests identified. 
This requires testers to prioritize tests such that important areas 
of concern are tested first.
The current practice in the industry is to identify feature 
interactions, based on the knowledge of behavior. While this is 
possible in the initial stages, it becomes difficult with time, as 
teams change and new members have lesser domain 
understanding. This manual process of identifying feature 
interactions has multiple issues: inability to achieve coverage, 
difficulty in prioritizing, dependency on experienced testers, 
and difficulty in measuring coverage.
spans.ResearchObjectives:
We developed an approach for feature interaction testing, 
and validated it by testing a site X.
spans.Context:
The highly competitive business environment of today has 
made it imperative that businesses are run in a cost-effective, 
agile and customer-centric manner. The need to reduce costs 
has lead to commoditization of software, while the need to 
adapt to customer-needs and frequent changes, has lead to 
software that is configurable or customizable. The result is, a 
new class of software, in which the software is configured or 
customized for every use. Some examples of such software are 
1) Internationalized software: customized for every country 2) 
ERP packages : customized for every organization where it is 
implemented 3) Consumer software products: personalized as 
per user preferences. In all the cases, both the number of 
variations and dimensions of variation tend to be very high, 
hence we categorize these as Variability Intensive Systems 
(VIS).
The software services industry is involved in the 
development, maintenance, testing and support of many such 
systems. Often, only a part of the service is allocated to an 
organization, while the rest may be done by the customer or 
another software service provider. This results in a variety of 
challenges that have been discussed in the next section.
spans.Goals:
We developed an approach for feature interaction testing, 
and validated it by testing a site X.
spans.ExperimentalMaterial:
Six portals of site X and an internationalized 
website similar to site X, were chosen for domain analysis. We 
also chose 6 features tested recently for test generation. ACTS 
[1] was selected as the combinatorial test generation tool.
spans.Procedure:
We first analyzed the domain to arrive at a 
feature model. Next we created perspectives by identifying 
common causes of variation. We identified the following 
perspectives:
Domain: This contains the core functionality features.
Internationalization: Since each portal is country specific, 
many features vary by country. Language, currency, 
measurement units are some features from this perspective.
Architecture: There were some domain features that could 
be configured with different architectural components. For 
example, the advertising module could be shown in the second 
column of a 2 page layout or on the third column of a 3 page 
layout. The advertising feature varies here by the page layout 
used. Similarly we observed variations in page themes, page 
types (like blog type, news article type) etc.
Operating Environment (OE): This includes features such 
as browsers, operating system, devices in which each domain 
feature has to function. While the functionality does not vary 
due to OE it is an inseparable part of the end user experience 
and may result in variations that are important to test. 
Accessibility: Certain accessibility features like zoom, 
scroll bars, default focus etc. are expected in certain features. 
These were modeled in this perspective.
A total of 150 features were created across all perspectives. 
This MPFM was used for configuring products. For our case, 
we consider each portal as a product configuration. We created 
portals corresponding to 3 countries for the purpose of our 
experiment.
Each perspective was passed as a parameter to ACTS. 
Features like language, browser, OS were also selected as 
parameters, since they were sources of variation for all 
features. The leaf nodes of the feature trees were used as values 
for the respective parameters. Since same feature combination 
could exist in multiple portals, portal was also passed as a 
parameter. The users had assigned an importance rating to the 
features. The generated combinations were prioritized such that 
the combinations with features of highest importance are above 
the ones with lesser importance.
spans.Summary:
We presented an approach of using Multi-Perspective 
Feature Models (MPFMs) and combinatorial testing to test 
feature interactions for a category of variability intensive 
systems viz. internationalized websites.
The approach was applied to a real-world case where we 
tested 6 different features of an internationalized web site. We 
found that about 65% of the test design effort and 37% of the 
test execution effort could be saved using our approach. Also, 
79% of defects from the live site could be reduced. The 
approach helped reduce dependency on experienced testers by 
modeling their knowledge of feature constraints and 
dependencies in the model.
In our opinion, there is a need for techniques to establish 
behavior relevance of features in order to identify more useful 
feature interactions to test. We also believe that the current 
practice of test case management leads to repetition of 
information in test cases and there is a need for new ways to 
model tests. Such test models can be used for variability 
modeling and can serve as basis for test activities like test 
selection, management, design and automation.
spans.FutureWork:
We also 
suggest that the research community perform more empirical 
studies, especially on defect data in order to motivate 
practitioners to adopt the state of the art techniques.

spans.Background: Locating source code elements relevant to a given fea-ture is an important step in the process of re-engineering software variants, developed by an ad-hoc reuse technique, into a Software Product Line (SPL) for systematic reuse. Existing works on using Information Retrieval (IR) tech-niques do not consider the abstraction gap between feature and source code levels. In our recent work, we have im-proved the effectiveness of IR-based feature location by in-troducing an intermediate level between feature and source code levels, called “code-topics”. We used Formal Con-cept Analysis (FCA) to identify such “code-topics” .
spans.Objective: In this paper, we investigate the results of using Agglomerative Hierarchical Clustering (AHC) algorithm to identify code-topics.
spans.Methods: experimental evaluation
spans.Results: In our experimental evaluation, we show that AHC signiﬁcantly increases the recall of feature location with a minor decrease of precision compared to FCA.
spans.ProblemStatement: Information Retrieval (IR) techniques have been widely used for feature location [5][6]. In our recent work [4], we have improved the effectiveness of IR-based feature lo-cation in a collection of product variants by bridging the abstraction gap between feature and source code levels. This bridging is performed by introducing an intermediate level, called code-topic. A code-topic is a cluster of simi-lar classes that reveal source code intention. A code-topic can be a functionality implemented by the source code and provided by a feature. In our recent work [4], we have com-bined a technique called Formal Concept Analysis (FCA) and IR to identify such code-topics.
spans.ResearchObjectives: In this paper, we propose to investigate the results of using Agglomerative Hierarchical Clustering (AHC) to identify “code-topics” .
spans.Context: Software product variants are a set of similar software products developed by ad-hoc copying with adaptations to meet new demands of customers [1]. They share some fea-tures, called mandatory features, and also support different, customer-speciﬁc features, called optional features. A fea-ture is “a prominent or distinctive user-visible aspect, qual-ity or characteristic of a software system” [2]. As numbers of variants and features grow, maintaining such software variants and developing new variants becomes more difﬁ-cult and expensive over time. Therefore, a transition to a systematic reuse approach, such as Software Product Line Engineering (SPLE) becomes necessary.
spans.Goals: we have proposed to combine IR and AHC to improve the effectiveness of IR-based feature location in a collection of product variants.
spans.ExperimentalUnits: we have applied it to a collec-tion of seven variants of a large-scale system, ArgoUML-SPL1 modeling tool, and ﬁve variants of a small-scale sys-tem, MobileMedia2.
spans.ExperimentalMaterial: two algorithms to identify code-topics: AHC (Agglomerative Hierarchical Clustering) and FCA (Formal Concept Analysis)
spans.Parameters: The most important parameter to LSI is the number of chosen term-topics. A term-topic is a collection of terms that co-occur frequently in the documents of the corpus. The proper way to make such a choice is an open issue in the literature. Too many term-topics leads to the association of irrelevant terms and too few term-topics leads to loosely relevant terms. We are unable to use a ﬁxed number of term-topics (#term-topics) because we have different sizes of code-topic documents. Therefore, we use a factor K be-tween 0.1 and 0.5. #term-topics is equal to (K × Ddim), where Ddim is the document dimensionality of the term-document matrix that is generated by LSI.
spans.IndependentVariables: AHC and FCA
spans.DependentVariables: precision, recall and F-measure
spans.Procedure: The ArgoUML-SPL is a Java open-source which sup-ports all standard UML 1.4 diagrams. The ArgoUML-SPL’s products are generated from the same framework so that products that share the same features also share the same code. The selected products differ in terms of provided fea-tures but they support all UML diagram features. These features are implemented by source code classes. To estab-lish ground truth links between features and their classes in order to evaluate our proposal, we compare code classes of two generated products; one of them provides all fea-tures while the other provides all features except the focused one. The obtained classes represent the real implementa-tion of the focused feature. We repeat this process for all ArgoUML-SPL’s features. MobileMedia is a JAVA open source that manipulates multimedia on mobile devices. In our study, we have considered and analyzed variants that only implement features as classes. To establish ground truth links between features and their source code classes, we analyze manually the source code.
spans.Summary: In this paper, we have proposed to combine IR and AHC to improve the effectiveness of IR-based feature location in a collection of product variants. This improvement involves reducing the abstraction gap between feature and source code levels by introducing the concept of code-topic as an intermediate level. We have compared between two algo-rithms to identify code-topics: AHC and FCA. In our ex-perimental evaluation using two different case studies, we showed that AHC signiﬁcantly increases the recall of IR-based feature location with a minor decrease of precision compared to FCA.

spans.Background:
Hidden code dependencies are responsible for many complications
in maintenance tasks. With the introduction of variable features in
conﬁgurable systems, dependencies may even cross feature bound-
aries, causing problems that are prone to be detected late. Many
current implementation techniques for product lines lack proper
interfaces, which could make such dependencies explicit.
spans.Objective:
As al-
ternative to changing the implementation approach, we provide a
tool-based solution to support developers in recognizing and dealing
with feature dependencies: emergent interfaces.
spans.Methods:
To evaluate the potential of emergent interfaces, we conducted and
replicated a controlled experiment
spans.Results:
To evaluate the potential of emergent interfaces, we conducted and
replicated a controlled experiment, and found, in the studied context,
that emergent interfaces can improve performance of code change
tasks by up to 3 times while also reducing the number of errors.
spans.ProblemStatement:
In such context, developers can easily
miss cross-feature dependencies, such as a feature assigning a value
to a variable read by another feature. As there is no mutual agree-
ment [48] between separate feature developers, changing one feature
might be the correct action for maintaining that feature, but might
bring undesirable consequences to the behavior of other features.
Similar issues could also appear when developers assume invalid
dependencies, as would be the case if the just discussed features
were mutually exclusive. In a prior study collecting metrics of 43
large-scale open-source implementations in which features were
implemented using the C preprocessor, we found that cross-feature
dependencies are frequent in practice [38].
spans.ResearchObjectives:
In particular, we evaluate emer-
gent interfaces by answering two research questions: Do emergent
interfaces reduce effort during code-change tasks involving feature-
code dependencies in preprocessor-based systems? Do emergent
interfaces reduce the number of errors during code-change tasks in-
volving feature-code dependencies in preprocessor-based systems?
spans.Context:
During maintenance, developers often introduce errors into soft-
ware systems when they fail to recognize module and feature depen-
dencies [10]. This problem is particularly critical for conﬁgurable
systems, in which features can be enabled and disabled at compile
time or run time, and market and technical needs constrain how
features can be combined. In this context, features often cross-
cut each other [29] and share program elements like variables and
methods [38], without proper modularity support from a notion of
interface between features.
spans.Goals:
Our evaluation aims to compare maintenance of preprocessor-
based product lines with and without emergent interfaces (these are
our treatments). Speciﬁcally, we are interested in the interaction
with the feature-hiding facilities of virtual separation of concerns,
which we enable in both cases to aid comprehensibility.
spans.ExperimentalUnits:
We performed the experiment three times. In a ﬁrst pilot study,
we tested the experimental design with a small group of six graduate
students at the University of Marburg, Germany. Next, we per-
formed the actual experiment with 10 graduate students—attendants
of a course on experimental software engineering lead by an in-
dependent lecturer—at Federal University of Pernambuco, Brazil
(Round 1). Finally, we replicated the experiment with 14 UROP
(Undergraduate Research Opportunity Program) students at Federal
University of Alagoas, Brazil (Round 2). In both rounds, around
half of the participants were part-time students with professional
experience—varying from few months to many years of experience.
All participants were informed they could stop participating at any
time, but nobody did.
spans.ExperimentalMaterial:
We use two preprocessor-based product lines as experimental
material: Best Lap and MobileMedia. The former is a highly-
conﬁgurable commercial product line that has about 15 KLOC.
The latter, which has about 3 KLOC, is an academic product line
for applications that manipulate photo, music, and video on mobile
devices [14]. It contains feature restrictions and has been used in
previous studies [14, 36]. ... We provide the product line’s source
code and corresponding tasks that the participants should perform
by modifying the source code.
spans.Tasks:
We provide a task of each kind for each product line, for a total of four distinct tasks, as discussed next.
Task 1 - New requirement for Best Lap. The new requirement
for Best Lap is similar to our motivating Scenario 1: There are
two methods of feature ARENA that contain conditional statements
forbidding negative scores. So, to accomplish the task, besides
changing the totalScore assignment, participants should remove
or rewrite these conditional statements (see one of them in method
setScore of Figure 1). To reach them, participants need to consider
interprocedural dependencies. That is, there are cross-feature depen-
dencies from the maintenance point to two conditional statements,
each one in a different method. In case Emergo is available, the
participant should use it to identify the cross-feature dependencies
between totalScore and the rest of the code. Otherwise, the partic-
ipant is free to use standard tools like ﬁnd/replace and highlighting.
This setup also holds for the subsequent tasks.
Task 2 - New requirement for MobileMedia. The task for
MobileMedia is conceptually similar in the sense that participants
should change a variable assignment, follow cross-feature depen-
dencies, and update conditional statements (here, only one if state-
ment). However, in contrast to Task 1, where the method call depth
to reach the two conditional statements is 1, here the call depth is 2.
That is, from the maintenance point, we need to follow two method
calls to reach the if statement.
Task 3 - Unused variable in Best Lap. In Best Lap, we asked
participants to ﬁx unused-variable warnings for two variables: tires
and xP. We introduced the bugs ourself by removing correct #ifdef
directives around the variable declarations. We can solve all unused-
variable tasks by following intraprocedural dependencies only, but
they typically require investigating code of different features. To
accomplish the tasks, we ask participants to put a correct #ifdef
around the variable declarations. The variables tires and xP are
inside methods with 147 and 216 source lines of code, respectively.
Task 4 - Unused variable in MobileMedia. Again the Mobile-
Media task is conceptually similar to the Best Lap task. Participants
should ﬁx the unused-variable warning of numberOfViews and
albumMusic. The two variables are placed in shorter methods
when compared to Task 3: they have 49 and 71 lines of code.
Overall, the tasks for both product lines have similarities, but
they are not equivalent. Actually, these differences—methods size,
method call depths to reach the impacted feature, and number of
conditionals to change—between tasks for both product lines help
us to better analyze the effects of our two treatments and is properly
controlled by our experiment design, as we shall see in Section 4.5.
Finally, we designed warmup tasks on a toy product line so that
participants could learn how to use Emergo at the start of the experi-
ment. We performed warmup tasks together in a class context but
did not evaluate their results.
spans.Hypotheses:
(H1 - Effort) With emergent interfaces, developers spend less
time to complete code-change tasks involving feature dependencies
in both product lines. (H2 - Error introduction) With emergent
interfaces, developers commit less errors in both product lines when
performing code-change tasks involving feature dependencies.
spans.IndependentVariables:
We distinguish between participants
using our treatments (independent variable with two levels: with and
without emergent interfaces). Additionally, we distinguish between
the tasks of both product lines, as we cannot assume equivalence
(independent variable with two levels: Best Lap and MobileMedia
tasks).
spans.DependentVariables:
We measure time and the number of errors (dependent
variables) for new-requirement tasks and unused-variable tasks.
spans.Procedure:
After randomly assigning each participant into our Latin Square
design, we distribute task-description sheets accordingly. Each par-
ticipant performs two tasks in two individually prepared installations
of Eclipse (with Emergo installed or not, with Best Lap or Mobile-
Media prepared readily as a project); each installation corresponds
to a cell of our Latin Square design. By preparing the Eclipse instal-
lation, we prevent participants from using Emergo when they are
not supposed to (it is simply not installed in that case). All Eclipse
installations support virtual separation, where we leave the ﬁrst line
with the #ifdef statement to inform the user of hidden code). Also
for the warmup tasks, we prepared a distinct Eclipse installation.
All tasks focus around a speciﬁc maintenance point (a variable
assignment). Since we are not interested in the time needed to locate
the variable, we prepare the installations in such a way that the
correct ﬁles are opened and the cursor is positioned exactly at the
maintenance point. ... At the start of the experiment session, we introduce preprocessors,
the hiding facilities of virtual separation of concerns, and emergent
interfaces. Together with the participants, we perform a warmup
task that uses Emergo. We introduce how to use the Play/Pause and
Finish buttons. For the entire experiment, we scheduled 2.5 hours
(training, warmup, and execution).
spans.AnalysisProcedure:
As analysis procedure for this design, we perform an ANOVA.
To give relevance to the ANOVA [6], we use the Bartlett, Box Cox,
and Tukey tests to verify variance homogeneity, normal distribution,
and model additivity, respectively. We follow the convention of
considering a factor as signiﬁcant when p-value < 0.05.
spans.Summary:
In this paper, we present emergent interfaces that emulate miss-
ing interfaces in many product-line implementations. We provide
Emergo, a complete version of a tool capable of inferring interfaces
from data-ﬂow analysis on demand. Emergent interfaces raise aware-
ness of cross-feature dependencies that are critical for maintaining
(conﬁgurable) software systems. With a conducted and replicated
controlled experiment, we evaluate to what extent such tool sup-
port can help achieving better feature modularization. Our study
focuses on feature-code-change tasks in product lines implemented
with preprocessors, since they are the prevalent way to implement
variable software in industrial practice. We observe a signiﬁcant
decrease in code-change effort by emergent interfaces, when faced
with interprocedural dependencies. Similarly, our study suggests a
reduction in errors made during those code-change tasks.
spans.FutureWork:
In future work, we will focus on scaling the underlying data-ﬂow analysis by
trading off performance and precision, and investigating emergent
interfaces for other implementation techniques.

{
  "Background": "Hidden code dependencies are responsible for many complications
in maintenance tasks. With the introduction of variable features in
conﬁgurable systems, dependencies may even cross feature bound-
aries, causing problems that are prone to be detected late. Many
current implementation techniques for product lines lack proper
interfaces, which could make such dependencies explicit.",
  "Objective": "As al-
ternative to changing the implementation approach, we provide a
tool-based solution to support developers in recognizing and dealing
with feature dependencies: emergent interfaces.",
  "Methods": "To evaluate the potential of emergent interfaces, we conducted and
replicated a controlled experiment",
  "Results": "To evaluate the potential of emergent interfaces, we conducted and
replicated a controlled experiment, and found, in the studied context,
that emergent interfaces can improve performance of code change
tasks by up to 3 times while also reducing the number of errors.",
  "ProblemStatement": "In such context, developers can easily
miss cross-feature dependencies, such as a feature assigning a value
to a variable read by another feature. As there is no mutual agree-
ment [48] between separate feature developers, changing one feature
might be the correct action for maintaining that feature, but might
bring undesirable consequences to the behavior of other features.
Similar issues could also appear when developers assume invalid
dependencies, as would be the case if the just discussed features
were mutually exclusive. In a prior study collecting metrics of 43
large-scale open-source implementations in which features were
implemented using the C preprocessor, we found that cross-feature
dependencies are frequent in practice [38].",
  "ResearchObjectives": "In particular, we evaluate emer-
gent interfaces by answering two research questions: Do emergent
interfaces reduce effort during code-change tasks involving feature-
code dependencies in preprocessor-based systems? Do emergent
interfaces reduce the number of errors during code-change tasks in-
volving feature-code dependencies in preprocessor-based systems?",
  "Context": "During maintenance, developers often introduce errors into soft-
ware systems when they fail to recognize module and feature depen-
dencies [10]. This problem is particularly critical for conﬁgurable
systems, in which features can be enabled and disabled at compile
time or run time, and market and technical needs constrain how
features can be combined. In this context, features often cross-
cut each other [29] and share program elements like variables and
methods [38], without proper modularity support from a notion of
interface between features.",
  "Goals": "Our evaluation aims to compare maintenance of preprocessor-
based product lines with and without emergent interfaces (these are
our treatments). Speciﬁcally, we are interested in the interaction
with the feature-hiding facilities of virtual separation of concerns,
which we enable in both cases to aid comprehensibility.",
  "ExperimentalUnits": "We performed the experiment three times. In a ﬁrst pilot study,
we tested the experimental design with a small group of six graduate
students at the University of Marburg, Germany. Next, we per-
formed the actual experiment with 10 graduate students—attendants
of a course on experimental software engineering lead by an in-
dependent lecturer—at Federal University of Pernambuco, Brazil
(Round 1). Finally, we replicated the experiment with 14 UROP
(Undergraduate Research Opportunity Program) students at Federal
University of Alagoas, Brazil (Round 2). In both rounds, around
half of the participants were part-time students with professional
experience—varying from few months to many years of experience.
All participants were informed they could stop participating at any
time, but nobody did.",
  "ExperimentalMaterial": "We use two preprocessor-based product lines as experimental
material: Best Lap and MobileMedia. The former is a highly-
conﬁgurable commercial product line that has about 15 KLOC.
The latter, which has about 3 KLOC, is an academic product line
for applications that manipulate photo, music, and video on mobile
devices [14]. It contains feature restrictions and has been used in
previous studies [14, 36]. ... We provide the product line’s source
code and corresponding tasks that the participants should perform
by modifying the source code.",
  "Tasks": "We provide a task of each kind for each product line, for a total of four distinct tasks, as discussed next.
Task 1 - New requirement for Best Lap. The new requirement
for Best Lap is similar to our motivating Scenario 1: There are
two methods of feature ARENA that contain conditional statements
forbidding negative scores. So, to accomplish the task, besides
changing the totalScore assignment, participants should remove
or rewrite these conditional statements (see one of them in method
setScore of Figure 1). To reach them, participants need to consider
interprocedural dependencies. That is, there are cross-feature depen-
dencies from the maintenance point to two conditional statements,
each one in a different method. In case Emergo is available, the
participant should use it to identify the cross-feature dependencies
between totalScore and the rest of the code. Otherwise, the partic-
ipant is free to use standard tools like ﬁnd/replace and highlighting.
This setup also holds for the subsequent tasks.
Task 2 - New requirement for MobileMedia. The task for
MobileMedia is conceptually similar in the sense that participants
should change a variable assignment, follow cross-feature depen-
dencies, and update conditional statements (here, only one if state-
ment). However, in contrast to Task 1, where the method call depth
to reach the two conditional statements is 1, here the call depth is 2.
That is, from the maintenance point, we need to follow two method
calls to reach the if statement.
Task 3 - Unused variable in Best Lap. In Best Lap, we asked
participants to ﬁx unused-variable warnings for two variables: tires
and xP. We introduced the bugs ourself by removing correct #ifdef
directives around the variable declarations. We can solve all unused-
variable tasks by following intraprocedural dependencies only, but
they typically require investigating code of different features. To
accomplish the tasks, we ask participants to put a correct #ifdef
around the variable declarations. The variables tires and xP are
inside methods with 147 and 216 source lines of code, respectively.
Task 4 - Unused variable in MobileMedia. Again the Mobile-
Media task is conceptually similar to the Best Lap task. Participants
should ﬁx the unused-variable warning of numberOfViews and
albumMusic. The two variables are placed in shorter methods
when compared to Task 3: they have 49 and 71 lines of code.
Overall, the tasks for both product lines have similarities, but
they are not equivalent. Actually, these differences—methods size,
method call depths to reach the impacted feature, and number of
conditionals to change—between tasks for both product lines help
us to better analyze the effects of our two treatments and is properly
controlled by our experiment design, as we shall see in Section 4.5.
Finally, we designed warmup tasks on a toy product line so that
participants could learn how to use Emergo at the start of the experi-
ment. We performed warmup tasks together in a class context but
did not evaluate their results.",
  "Hypotheses": "(H1 - Effort) With emergent interfaces, developers spend less
time to complete code-change tasks involving feature dependencies
in both product lines. (H2 - Error introduction) With emergent
interfaces, developers commit less errors in both product lines when
performing code-change tasks involving feature dependencies.",
  "IndependentVariables": "We distinguish between participants
using our treatments (independent variable with two levels: with and
without emergent interfaces). Additionally, we distinguish between
the tasks of both product lines, as we cannot assume equivalence
(independent variable with two levels: Best Lap and MobileMedia
tasks).",
  "DependentVariables": "We measure time and the number of errors (dependent
variables) for new-requirement tasks and unused-variable tasks.",
  "Procedure": "After randomly assigning each participant into our Latin Square
design, we distribute task-description sheets accordingly. Each par-
ticipant performs two tasks in two individually prepared installations
of Eclipse (with Emergo installed or not, with Best Lap or Mobile-
Media prepared readily as a project); each installation corresponds
to a cell of our Latin Square design. By preparing the Eclipse instal-
lation, we prevent participants from using Emergo when they are
not supposed to (it is simply not installed in that case). All Eclipse
installations support virtual separation, where we leave the ﬁrst line
with the #ifdef statement to inform the user of hidden code). Also
for the warmup tasks, we prepared a distinct Eclipse installation.
All tasks focus around a speciﬁc maintenance point (a variable
assignment). Since we are not interested in the time needed to locate
the variable, we prepare the installations in such a way that the
correct ﬁles are opened and the cursor is positioned exactly at the
maintenance point. ... At the start of the experiment session, we introduce preprocessors,
the hiding facilities of virtual separation of concerns, and emergent
interfaces. Together with the participants, we perform a warmup
task that uses Emergo. We introduce how to use the Play/Pause and
Finish buttons. For the entire experiment, we scheduled 2.5 hours
(training, warmup, and execution).",
  "AnalysisProcedure": "As analysis procedure for this design, we perform an ANOVA.
To give relevance to the ANOVA [6], we use the Bartlett, Box Cox,
and Tukey tests to verify variance homogeneity, normal distribution,
and model additivity, respectively. We follow the convention of
considering a factor as signiﬁcant when p-value < 0.05.",
  "Summary": "In this paper, we present emergent interfaces that emulate miss-
ing interfaces in many product-line implementations. We provide
Emergo, a complete version of a tool capable of inferring interfaces
from data-ﬂow analysis on demand. Emergent interfaces raise aware-
ness of cross-feature dependencies that are critical for maintaining
(conﬁgurable) software systems. With a conducted and replicated
controlled experiment, we evaluate to what extent such tool sup-
port can help achieving better feature modularization. Our study
focuses on feature-code-change tasks in product lines implemented
with preprocessors, since they are the prevalent way to implement
variable software in industrial practice. We observe a signiﬁcant
decrease in code-change effort by emergent interfaces, when faced
with interprocedural dependencies. Similarly, our study suggests a
reduction in errors made during those code-change tasks.",
  "FutureWork": "In future work, we will focus on scaling the underlying data-ﬂow analysis by
trading off performance and precision, and investigating emergent
interfaces for other implementation techniques."
}

spans.Background: Despite the wide use of software product lines, their imple-mentation and evolution is a challenging task. When im-plementing a feature, a developer has to know which codefragments of other (already implemented) features are ac-cessible in each program variant in which the feature is in-cluded.Especially for composition-based implementationtechniques, in which the code is implemented in separatedmodules, it is an exhausting and error-prone task to ﬁndsafely accessible code fragments of other modules. State-of-the-art tool support, such as product-line type checkers, de-tect errors a posteriori (i.e., during compilation), but fails toprevent errors during the implementation.
spans.Objective: To overcome this problem, we propose feature-context interfaces, which pro-vide a modular and non-variable programming interface tothe variable source code of a product line. These interfacesease changes, extensions, and the maintainability of productlines.
spans.Methods: To demonstrate applicability, we implemented a con-tent assist and an outline view in Eclipse based on feature-context interfaces. We evaluate the potential of our methodby analyzing the number of potential type errors we preventcompared to state-of-the-art techniques.
spans.ProblemStatement: In general, how can the developer know which methods exist and are safely callable from a certain feature? The de-veloper needs to consider the domain dependencies amongfeatures in the SPL (e.g., one feature requires another fea-ture) and has to infer from these dependencies all accessiblecode fragments. With an increasing number of features andtheir dependencies, this approach quickly becomes infeasi-ble. To the best of our knowledge, there is no approach thatsupports the developer and presents a modular and non-var-iable view on safely reusable code fragments for a currentlyimplemented module.
spans.ResearchObjectives: We propose an interface depending on the current featurecontext. The feature context represents the feature in whichthe developer is working to extend, maintain, or changethe SPL. Based on this context, we compute a non-variableinterface, called feature-context interface, to the remainingcode of the SPL that is safely accessible. By using membersof the interface only, we are able to prevent compile-timeerrors before the compilation and we are aware of reuse op-portunities.
spans.Context: Software product-line (SPL) engineering aims at the de-velopment of similar programs based on a common codebase [8]. Features describe the commonalities and variabili-ties of di↵erent program variants [10]. To generate a tailoredprogram, called variant, stakeholders select features, satis-fying their requirements. Selected features are mapped totheir corresponding implementation units, which are thencomposed and compiled to obtain customized program vari-ants. The beneﬁts of reduced time-to-market and high re-usability led to the development of an increasing number ofSPLs in practice, such as HP printer driver, Siemens medicalcare SPL, the Linux kernel, and Nokia’s SPLs [24].
spans.Goals:
To quantify the prevention of potential errors of feature-context interface against state-of-the-art approaches (see Sec-tion 3), we conducted an empirical study with two goals inmind:
(a) We analyze whether state-of-the-art approaches presentincomplete or unsound results for existing SPLs.
(b) We quantify how evident potential errors are in exist-ing SPLs.
spans.ExperimentalMaterial:
Our evaluation is based on eight feature-oriented SPLs written in Java taken from publicly available repositories.1
These SPLs are selected from di↵erent do-mains with di↵erent sizes in terms of the derivable variantsand the number of features. All SPLs exhibit no compile-time errors in all valid variants. Furthermore, these SPLswere used in previous studies by other researchers and canbe considered as a benchmark in SPL analysis [3, 15, 23].In detail, we use two graph libraries GPL and GraphLib, twogames TankWar and GameOfLife, the text editor Notepad,the chat client PKJab, the search engine DesktopSearcher,and the compression library ZipMe as subject SPLs (see Ta-ble 2).
spans.Procedure:
To compare each state-of-the-art approach to the feature-context interface, we investigate a typical implementationscenario of a developer in which a feature module is to beextended by new functionality.
(a) Incomplete or Unsound Results. The experimentalprocedure to address goal (a) is as follows: we select eachfeature of an SPL as the feature context and compute foreach approach the number of all accessible members. Weconsider the approaches described in Section 3: feature mod-ule, minimal variant, and always available. In addition, weuse the feature context to determine the existing members inthe feature-context interface. We determine the number ofexisting members in the variable interface VInt and scale theresults of all approaches to this set of members, to achievevisually comparable results.
As mentioned in Section 3, the result of the approach min-imal variant heavily depends on the selection of a speciﬁcvariant. It is possible that two or more variants are mini-mal variants related to their number of features but containdi↵erent sets of members. To represent the number of mem-bers for the approach minimal variant, we select for eachfeature context a minimal variant that results in the mini-mum number of members.
(b) Potential Errors. The experimental procedure to ad-dress goal (b) is similar. First, we compute for each approachand feature context all accessible members. In contrast toprocedure (a), we consider not only the number of accessiblemembers, but compare the resulting members directly withthe members of the feature-context interface. If a member isavailable in an approach but not part of the feature-contextinterface, we count this member as a potential error lead-ing to compile-time errors in the implementation. Thus, allerrors that we count for the minimal variant are potentialcompile-time errors. By contrast, each member that is avail-able in the feature-context interface but not part of a spe-ciﬁc approach e↵ectively limits reuse opportunities. There-fore, we count each non-existing member in the approachesfeature module and always available also as a potential er-ror. For illustration purposes, we also scale the number ofcounted errors for each approach to the number of membersin the variable interface VInt. This allows us to summa-rize the counted errors for each approach about all subjectsystems. As result, we reason about the potential of feature-context interface compared to state-of-the-art approaches.In contrast to the procedure (a), we investigate all minimalvariants related to a feature context and include the resultsin our evaluation. This allows us to identify all possible errorsthat can occur only in one of all minimal variants.
spans.Summary: Software product-line (SPL) engineering facilitates the gen-eration of similar program variants based on a common codebase. Although many approaches exist dealing with the im-plementation of SPLs, their development is still far fromtrivial, especially for composition-based implementation tech-niques. Previous research aimed at the detection of compile-time errors, whereas we aim to prevent errors. In detail, ifthe developer knows which code is safe to access relatedto the currently implemented feature (i.e., the feature con-text), compile-time errors, such as dangling references, canbe avoided up-front.We propose feature-context interfaces that provide a non-variable view to all safely accessible code in a given fea-ture context. Based on feature-context interfaces, we imple-mented a content assist and an outline view in FeatureIDE.We evaluated our approach using a set of publicly availableSPLs. In these SPLs, we found that only feature-contextinterfaces can provide exactly all members that are safe toaccess (not more and not less).
spans.FutureWork: In future work, we extend our tool support for feature-con-text interfaces so that it can be used as well for annotation-based approaches and for suggestions of new feature depen-dencies. For instance, if a developer wants to use code thatis not accessible in a current feature context, we proposenew constraints to the feature model to change the accessi-bility. Furthermore, based on the results of our evaluation,we plan to conduct a user study to investigate di↵erencesin development time and occurrences of errors when usingfeature-context interfaces compared to state-of-the-art tech-niques.

spans.Background: Software Product Line Engineering (SPLE) is a systematic reuse approach to develop a short time-to-market and quality products, called Software Product Line (SPL). Usually, a SPL is not developed from scratch but it is developed by reusing features (resp. their implementing source code elements) of existing similar systems previously developed by ad-hoc reuse techniques. The features implementations that are reused may be changed for developing new products (SPL) using SPLE. Any code element can be a part of (shared by) di®erent features implementations; modifying one feature's implementation can thus impact others. Therefore, feature-level Change Impact Analysis (CIA) is important to predict a®ected features for change management pur- pose.
spans.Objective: In this paper, we propose a feature-level CIA approach using Formal Concept Analysis (FCA) applied to SPL evolution.
spans.Methods: In our experimental evaluation using three case studies of di®erent domains and sizes,
spans.Results: In our experimental evaluation using three case studies of di®erent domains and sizes, we show the e®ectiveness of our technique in terms of the most commonly used metrics on the subject.
spans.ProblemStatement: Feature-level CIA is far from a trivial task when we have a large number of features. Manually tracing feature implementations to determine a®ected features is time-consuming, error-prone and tedious. The CIA is seldom considered at the fea- ture level for changes made to the source code level. Most of the existing works performs CIA at the source code level with little works completed at requirement and design levels [6].
spans.ResearchObjectives: In this article, we propose a feature-level CIA based on Formal Concept Analysis (FCA). The proposed approach mainly takes, as input, a change set composed of classes to be changed and computes, as output, a ranked list of a®ected features. Each feature in the ranked list has a degree to be a®ected repre- senting the feature priority to be checked by maintainers. Additionally, we propose two metrics to support feature level CIA: impact degree and changeability assess- ment metrics. The former is used to measure to which degree a speci¯c feature can be a®ected. The latter is used to measure the percentage of features that are a®ected.
spans.Context: SPLE is an engineering discipline providing methods to promote systematic software reuse for developing short time-to-market and quality products in a cost-e±cient way [1]. These products are referred to as Software Product Lines (SPLs) [1]. A SPL is "a set of software-intensive systems sharing a common, managed set of features that satisfy the speci¯c needs of a particular market segment or mission and that are developed from a common set of core assets in a prescribed way" [1]. The whole idea behind SPLE is to build core assets consisting of all reusable software artifacts (such as source code, test cases and so on) that can be leveraged to develop SPL product. Building such core assets is driven by features that SPL products should provide. A feature is "a prominent or distinctive user-visible aspect, quality or char- acteristic of a software system" [2].
spans.Goals: proved the e®ectiveness of our approach
spans.ExperimentalUnits: our feature-level CIA approach
spans.ExperimentalMaterial:
We have applied it to core assets of three di®erent case studies: ArgoUML-SPLa, MobileMediab and BerkelyDB-SPL.c
The MobileMedia is a JAVA open source software which manipulates multimedia on mobile devices. It was implemented in 8 subsequent releases, each incorporates new mandatory, optional or alternative features. These features are implemented by adding source code classes or modifying already existing classes. The core assets of MobileMedia supports 6 features such as, view photo, delete photo, sort photos, etc.
ArgoUML-SPL is a large-scale system. It is a JAVA open-source which supports all standard UML diagrams. The core assets of ArgoUML-SPL supports 8 features such as, the Class diagram, the State diagram, the Activity diagram, etc. ... BerkeleyDB-SPL is an open source database engine, entirely implemented in JAVA. It can work as a standalone database (run as .jar ¯le), or be embedded as a third party library in the JAVA application. It provides the embedded storage, with open interfaces designed for programmers. Originally, BerkeleyDB was a single ap- plication, but Kastner and others have re-engineered it as a SPL [20]. Core assets of BerkeleyDB-SPL implement (42) features. Most of these features are implemented by low source code granularity (such as methods) [20]. There are only (25) features that their associated classes are known and available.d Therefore, we create core assets only containing these features.
spans.IndependentVariables: change set of classes (CSC )
spans.DependentVariables: We relied on three measures from information retrieval, namely precision, recall and F-measure to evaluate our CIA approach [21, 22]. Precision measures the accuracy of the estimated a®ected features according to the actual a®ected features. Recall measures to what degree the estimated a®ected features covers the actual a®ected features. F-measure makes a trade-o® between precision and recall, so that it gives a high value only in the case that both recall and precision values are high.
spans.Procedure: In this section, we provide an experimental evaluation of our feature-level CIA ap- proach to demonstrate its feasibility. We have applied it to core assets of three di®erent case studies: ArgoUML-SPLa, MobileMediab and BerkelyDB-SPL.c ... We relied on three measures from information retrieval, namely precision, recall and F-measure to evaluate our CIA approach [21, 22]. Precision measures the accuracy of the estimated a®ected features according to the actual a®ected features. Recall measures to what degree the estimated a®ected features covers the actual a®ected features. F-measure makes a trade-o® between precision and recall, so that it gives a high value only in the case that both recall and precision values are high. Based on the de¯nitions above, we can see that precision also quanti¯es a®ected features that actually are not a®ected (false-positive). Also, recall quanti¯es the features that are a®ected but not identi¯ed (false-negatives). In our study, we use the following de¯nitions of precision, recall and F-measure. ... If precision equals 1, this means that maintainers spend less time and e®ort to locate a®ected features. If recall equals 1, this gives maintainers the con¯dence that all of a®ected features have been considered.

spans.Background: Existing similar software variants, developed by ad-hoc reuse technique such as “clone-and-own” , represent a starting point to build a software product line (SPL) core assets. To re-engineer such legacy software variants into an SPL for systematic reuse, it is important to be able to identify a mapping between features and their implementing source code elements in different variants. Information Retrieval (IR) methods have been used widely to support this mapping in a single software product.
spans.Objective: This paper proposes a new approach to improve the performance of IR methods when they are applied to a collection of software variants.
spans.Methods: We have applied our approach to a collection of seven variants of a large-scale system by using the ArgoUML-SPL modeling tool.
spans.Results: The experimental results showed that our approach outperforms conventional application of IR methods as well as the most recent and relevant work on the subject.
spans.ProblemStatement: Traceability links are needed to understand product vari-ants code and automatically derive concrete products from SPL core assets by selecting features and consequently their corresponding source code. Information Retrieval (IR) methods have been widely accepted to automate traceability recovery in single software [2]. The conventional application of IR methods is to map all feature descriptions of a software product to its entire source code. These features and the associated source code are called IR search spaces.
spans.ResearchObjectives: In this paper, we propose a new approach to improve the performance of IR-based methods when they are ap-plied to identify feature-to-code traceability in a collection of object-oriented software variants. The novelty of our approach is twofold. First, it exploits commonalities and variabilities across product variants to reduce IR spaces. As a result, the accuracy of IR results increases by mapping less number of features to less implementation in order to prevent false positive links. Second, it increases the number of retrieved links that are relevant by reducing the abstraction gap between features and source code levels. This is achieved by introducing an intermediate level, called “code-topic” . A code-topic is a cluster of classes that are grouped together based on their textual contents. Using code-topics, we can get more relevant information (i.e., more identiﬁers) to textually match these classes together with a feature description. Such code-topics can be functionalities abstracted as a feature where we consider that a feature is a bundle of functionalities.
spans.Context: Software variants are a set of similar software products that share some features, called common features, and also differ in others, called optional features. A feature is a prominent or distinctive user-visible aspect, quality or characteristic of a software system or systems [1]. Software variants often are developed by ad-hoc reuse techniques such as “clone-and-own” where an existing product is copied and later modiﬁed to meet new demands of customers. When the number of variants and features increase such ad-hoc technique causes critical problems such as maintain-ing each variant individually and reuse features (i.e., their implementation) will become difﬁcult and time consuming. To overcome these problems, it is important to re-engineer these variants into software product line (SPL) for systematic reuse. To this end, it is important to be able to identify a mapping between features and their implementing source code elements (e.g., classes). This mapping is known as traceability links or feature location.
spans.Goals: To validate our approach
spans.ExperimentalMaterial: To validate our approach, we have applied it to seven variants of a large-scale system, ArgoUML-SPL1 modeling tool. ArgoUML-SPL is a Java open-source which supports all standard UML 1.4 diagrams. The variants support all ArgoUML-SPL features and are generated from the same framework so that variants which share some features also share the same code. They implement features at class level and real implementation for each feature is determined by preprocessor directives to delimit the code associated with each feature. To analyze the source code of these variants, we use JDT/DOM. For LSI we have implemented them according to the description in section II.C. For FCA, we depend on Galois sub-hierarchical (GSH2) tool.
spans.Parameters: The most important parameter to LSI is the number of chosen term-topics. A term-topic is a collection of terms that co-occur frequently in the documents of the corpus. We need enough term-topics to capture real term relations. Too many term-topics lead to associate irrelevant terms and too few term-topics lead to loose relevant terms. We cannot use a ﬁxed number of term-topics (#term-topics) for LSI, because we have different size of class sets. Thus, we use a factor K between 0.1 and 0.5 as well as between 0.01 and 0.05 to determine (#term-topics). It is equal to “k × Ddim”, where Ddim is the document dimensionality of the term-document matrix that is generated by LSI.
spans.DependentVariables: The effectiveness of IR methods is commonly measured by their precision, recall and F-measure.
spans.Procedure: To validate our approach, we have applied it to seven variants of a large-scale system, ArgoUML-SPL1 modeling tool.
spans.Summary: We presented in this paper a new approach which com-bines FCA with IR to establish traceability links between object-oriented source code of a collection of software variants and their features. The contribution of this paper is twofold. First, it improves the accuracy of IR results and second it increases the number of retrieved links that are relevant. The evaluation results show that our approach outperforms the conventional application of IR methods as well as the most recent and relevant work on the subject.
